8.3       Despite repeated suggestion to take urgent steps to complete the construction of 18 Youth Hostels that has been
under construction for years now, in some cases even 20 years, the Committee finds that the situation has not improved at
all.  Rather, the status has become worse as 2 more Youth Hostels has been added to the list of Youth Hostels under
construction.  The Committee finds this situation disappointing and strongly recommends the Ministry to take remedial
steps in this regard.
 
8.4       In response to the Committee's recommendation that specific action be initiated to remedy the problem of non
construction in 176
th Report of the Committee, the Ministry informed that it has taken remedial action for improvement in
the system by stopping release of approved funds till the identified plot is developed by the State Government and handed
over to CPWD or any other construction agency.   The Ministry has also decided to cancel the approval if the information
is not received.  In this process, the approval of Navegaon Youth Hostel in Maharashtra which was approved in principle
has been cancelled.   Ministry has also decided to recover the funds, released for the construction work where the
construction has not started.  In this process, DG, CPWD, New Delhi has been requested to refund the amount of Rs. 20.00
lakhs released to CPWD, Manipur for construction of Youth  Hostel at Bishnupur in Manipur.  The Ministry has now
decided to give priority to the on-going projects, and only thereafter will other approved projects be taken up.  No further
proposals are being approved or considered at present.  The Outcome Budget 2007-08 of the Ministry states its projected
outcomes are to complete the ongoing Youth Hostels and to start new Youth Hostels as per availability of funds.  While
agreeing with the Ministry's decision to firstly complete the ongoing construction of Youth Hostels, it expresses concern
over the inadequacy of funds since the budget earmarked for the languishing projects must have become insufficient in
relation to prevailing price index.  The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to complete the construction in a
time bound manner.  The Committee feels that the Ministry's target of completing the construction of six Youth Hostels
during this fiscal is quite low, it must be more.
 
8.5       The Committee's attention is drawn to the oft-repeated fact that failure to get a developed site from the State
Government is the main reason behind the delay.   However, the Committee has been informed that approval is given and
the funds under the Scheme is released only after examining a developed site which is handed over to the CPWD for
construction of Youth Hostel.  If it were so, the Committee fails to appreciate the problem of late or non-availability of
requisite site for the Hostels.  In this backdrop, the Committee desires the Ministry to furnish a note as to the factors that
have caused delay in construction of Youth Hostels, since such delays result in time and cost overruns.
 
8.6       The Ministry has informed that based on the deliberations in the Working Group for the XIth Plan, it has been
proposed to increase the number of Youth Hostels in the country from 72 to 200 during the 11
th Five Year Plan.  However,
the actual number of new hostels that can be constructed will depend on the outlay given to the Ministry of Youth Affairs
and Sports.  It is also mentioned that some structural changes regarding the management of so many Youth Hostels have
been proposed by the Working Group which, inter-alia  would include possible PPP bases module.   This suggestion is
being examined in the Ministry.  In the meanwhile the focus of attention will be on completion of the on-going projects. 
The Committee is of the view that the private participation should not be explored as the first option to overhaul and
correct the things. The Committee would like to have a copy of the proposals of the Working Group, particularly as
regards the suggestions on structural changes in the management of the Youth Hostels. 
 
8.7       The Committee takes note of the following assessment made by the Working Group for the Eleventh Plan-
-
         Areas of concern are selection of site, construction and actual functioning of the Hostels, many times sites are
selected without due consideration, resulting in hostels not being optimally utilised after construction.
-         Construction of Hostels takes an unduly long time due to cumbersome procedure.
-         Instances of hostels being used by other organisations for other purposes are also there.
-         Only a handful of Government owned Youth Hostels have got affiliation to the International Youth Hostel
Association as they fail to meet the prescribed standards on accommodation, reception, hygiene, security etc.
 
8.8       The Committee strongly feels that keeping in view the proposed expansion of Youth Hostels from 72 to 200 during
the Eleventh Plan, the above-mentioned shortcomings need serious attention.   The Committee accordingly recommends
that the Ministry should initiate corrective measures in respect of existing Hostels and also ensure that the proposed
Hostels do not have these problem areas.

for National Coaching Scheme and Plan Scheme staff and other facilities.   The situation is more grim in the case of

more than what was required.  This is a serious lapse.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to enquire into it and take
corrective measures immediately.
 
9.7       The Committee feels that the existing system of financial management in the SAI is weak and that needs to be
strengthened.  It has been the experience of the Committee that due to inadequate supervision/monitoring of the financial
affairs, instances of irregularities as well as adverse audit reports have been reported during the recent years.  The officials
looking after finance in the SAI are either over-burdened or are given responsibilities about which they do not have
relevant experience.  As a result, they are not able to spare required time for their main responsibility.  In view of the
above, the Committee feels that the person looking after finance should be given other responsibilities only when they are
able to fulfil their primary responsibility in an  effective and comprehensive manner.

XVI     GENERAL OBSERVATION
 
16.1     The Committee after going through the replies and other documents relating to Demands for Grants of various
years including that of 2007-08 arrives at conclusion that the financial performance/management of the Ministry leaves
much to be desired.  Importance of the mandate of the Ministry – development, empowerment of youth as well as
promotion of sports – can hardly be over-emphasized.  The Committee has all these years been pleading for more funds for
these purposes.  Rs. 200 crore for development of youth who constitute 45% of our population and on whom the country is
pinning all its hope for future, is just a peanut.   Similarly, sports development gets Rs. 350 crore + Rs. 150 crore for
Commonwealth Games, 2010.
 
16.2     On the other hand, the Committee regrets to say that even these meagre allocations are not being utilized
completely and properly.  Every year, crores of rupees are left as unspent balance or being allowed to lapse due to various
reasons-non-settlement of accounts and pending UCs being the two most important ones.  As a result, crores of rupees are
blocked every year and our schemes languish.  Another disturbing trend noticed in this regard is the quantum jump in
spending of allocations in March every year.  Such a position leads to a situation where we have plan, programmes and
targets but there is no performance.   Flow of funds from Centre to States and other implementing agencies take 8 to 10
months, at times more.  Some schemes are prepared/declared to be revised/redesigned before they actually take off.    The
Committee has no option but to conclude that our schemes are suffering not merely because of paucity of funds but also
because of problems in our delivery mechanism, the procedure we adopt and above all the attitude in the administrative
machinery.  Lack of effective mechanisms for monitoring, authentic feedback, objective evaluation, etc. make it difficult
to gauge the performance of a scheme. 
 
16.3     These are larger questions which need to be considered at various levels to evolve a system as well as culture in
which we work as facilitator/enabler also not only as a controller, which has an effective system of transparency and
accountability and enough scope for correction and improvement.
16.4     The Committee has been expressing its reservation about the transfer of Sports Infrastructure Scheme to the States. 
The Committee has noted the assurance of the Ministry to consider it in the ongoing exercises for the formulation of the
Eleventh Plan.  The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation in 176
th Report for strengthening of monitoring and
effective implementation rather than transferring the scheme to the States.

district as well as block level, how can these RITYDCs become an effective instrument in bridging digital gap, the
beneficiaries intended and their level of skill acquirement, etc. needs to be taken into account.   The Committee fears that
unless these things were thoroughly examined, the proposed reorientation in the XIth Plan may not have the desired
results.                                                                     (para 4.17)
 
            The Committee would like the Ministry to make all efforts for an early settlement of the case.  The Committee would
like to state that whenever the recruitment process is restarted, the candidates of the impugned recruitment process should be
given preference.                                                                               (para 4.19)
 
            Another related aspect is of the creation of new posts necessitated due to proposed expansion of NYKS in the
remaining districts of the country.  Besides, there are large number of vacancies that are waiting to be filled up.  In view of
this, the Committee finds that NYKS is currently highly short of manpower affecting thereby the implementation and
effectivity of its schemes adversely.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that these aspects need to be taken up on
priority, particularly with the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission, to expedite the creation of new as well as
recruitment of existing posts at various levels in NYKS.  (para 4.20)
            The Committee has learnt that the NYKS is being involved in the schemes/programmes not only of its parent
Ministry but also of other Ministries/Departments.  The Committee is of the opinion that the District Nehru Yuva Kendras
(NYKs) thereby face problem in fulfilling their primary mandate.   The Committee suggests that NYKS should be given
extra responsibilities only when there is a scope for it in terms of time, resource, expertise etc.                         (para 4.21)
 
V         RASHTRIYA SADBHAVANA YOJANA
 
            The Committee notes that the performance of the scheme of Rashtriya Sadbhavna Yojna has been uneven in
different states.   The Committee only hopes that the Ministry must have taken the matter of slow registration of clubs with
concerned States to resolve it.  The Committee, in view of practical problems being faced in selection of NYSs, regrets to
say that these problems still persist.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to take urgent steps to remove the
difficulties encountered in the actual selection of Nehru Yuva Sathees.                   (para 5.2)
 
            The committee welcomes this raise but is afraid that in the face of rising inflation and other factors, even this raise
may not be sufficient to encourage the volunteers to come forth as Nehru Yuva Sathis.  The Committee is of the opinion
that Rs. 1500 may not be at all adequate for areas like J&K, North-East, Himachal Pradesh and Uttrakhand.
                                                                            (para 5.3)

against a target of 250 programmes in 2005-06, only 18 programmes could be organized.   The Committee notes from the
Outcome Budget, 2007-08, that the reason for this low achievement is perhaps due to non-viable proposals coming from

            The Committee would like to know the reason as to why the latter programme was given more weightage than the
former one. The Committee recommends the Ministry to ensure that all the components of the scheme are given equal
emphasis.                                                                                             (para 6.6)
 
            The Committee also notes that the ratio between male and females participants is roughly 3:1 in both the
categories.  The Committee expresses its concern over the steep decline in the number of participants under this scheme
and it recommends that it needs to be increased substantially.  The Committee did not have the figures for the year 2006-
07.                                       (para 6.7)
 
            As regards the lower ratio of female participants, the Committee feels that the Ministry’s endeavour should be to
increase it to the level of their ratio in our total population.                                                                                  (para 6.8)
 
            The Committee is not happy with the level of Ministry's efforts to obtain pending UCs.  Simply publishing notices
in newspapers is not going to achieve anything.   It requires more active/concerted efforts by the Ministry as a facilitator.  
The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to get the pending UCs liquidated on urgent basis and at the same time
also ensure that there is no recurrence of such tendency in future.                                                      (para 6.9)
 
VII
       NATIONAL SERVICE VOLUNTEERS SCHEME
 
            The Committee welcomes the enhancement in the stipends of the volunteers but it still feels that this enhancement
is not sufficient, given the fact that as NSVs, they contribute significantly for social work on a full time basis. The
Committee recommends further enhancement in the stipend of the Volunteers.  (para 7.3)
 
            The Committee notes that there is a little awareness about the existence of such a scheme in the public.   The
Committee emphasizes the need for giving a wider publicity about the scheme, mode of recruitment of volunteers, etc.
(para 7.5)
            The Committee further notes that 30 per cent of NSVs after the training remain unemployed and only 30 per cent
become social worker.  The Committee feels that with this achievement, the scheme has failed to create a desirable impact
on our youth particularly to join social sector in a big way.              (para 7.6)
 
            The Committee notes that these NSVs are associated with NYKs.  However, given the fact that only 500 districts in
the country have NYKs, the youth of remaining districts are being deprived of the opportunity to become NSVs.   Further,
with the projection of only 4400 NSVs to be deployed during 2007-08, the number of volunteers for a district comes to
mere 8 volunteers per district.  The Committee feels that this is an inadequate number.  It only hopes that NSVs are being
selected from uncovered districts as well.                                                                        (para 7.7)

            Despite repeated suggestion to take urgent steps to complete the construction of 18 Youth Hostels that has been

            While agreeing with the Ministry's decision to firstly complete the ongoing construction of Youth Hostels, it

insufficient in relation to prevailing price index.  The Committee strongly recommends the Ministry to complete the
construction in a time bound manner.  The Committee feels that the Ministry's target of completing the construction of six
Youth Hostels during this fiscal is quite low, it must be more.                    (para 8.4)
 
            If it were so, the Committee fails to appreciate the problem of late or non-availability of requisite site for the
Hostels.  In this backdrop, the Committee desires the Ministry to furnish a note as to the factors that have caused delay in
construction of Youth Hostels, since such delays result in time and cost overruns.(para 8.5)
 
            The Committee is of the view that the private participation should not be explored as the first option to overhaul
and correct the things. The Committee would like to have a copy of the proposals of the Working Group, particularly as
regards the suggestions on structural changes in the management of the Youth Hostels.               (para 8.6)
            The Committee strongly feels that keeping in view the proposed expansion of Youth Hostels from 72 to 200 during
the Eleventh Plan, the above-mentioned shortcomings need serious attention.   The Committee accordingly recommends
that the Ministry should initiate corrective measures in respect of existing Hostels and also ensure that the proposed
Hostels do not have these problem areas.(para 8.8)
IX        SPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA (SAI)
 
            The Committee is not happy at the unspent balance becoming a recurring feature in the SAI.  The underutilization
of Plan funds must have affected various programmes/schemes being run by SAI for promotion of sports in the country. 
The Committee feels that this also must have hindered the attainment of excellence in various sports.  The Committee
strongly recommends the Ministry to ensure that SAI utilizes the Plan funds completely on time and in proper manner.
(para 9.3)
            But the Committee is constrained to conclude that SAI could have achieved more than what it has till date.         
                                                            (para 9.4)
            The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the slow pace of utilization of funds under all the schemes, except
for National Coaching Scheme and Plan Scheme staff and other facilities.   The situation is more grim in the case of
schemes like National Sports Talent Contest, Special Area Games, Centres of Excellence, Sports Science/Medical Centre
& Research Scholarship, Central Pool of Technical sports Equipment, SAI Housing complex, Indira Gandhi Stadium,
Computerized Sports Data Band and infrastructure Development & Capital Works.  The Committee fails to understand
that in case of some of the Schemes, although the expenditure is less than 50 per cent, the physical targets have been either
achieved or are close to it.  This suggests that either the targets fixed were not realistic or allocation to the scheme were
more than what was required.  This is a serious lapse.  The Committee recommends the Ministry to enquire into it and take
corrective measures immediately.                                                                                                             (para 9.6)
 
            The Committee feels that the existing system of financial management in the SAI is weak and that needs to be
strengthened.  It has been the experience of the Committee that due to inadequate supervision/monitoring of the financial

affairs, instances of irregularities as well as adverse audit reports have been reported during the recent years.  The officials
looking after finance in the SAI are either over-burdened or are given responsibilities about which they do not have

TEAMS Division
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that though some success has been achieved at international level, yet we have a

            The Committee recommends the Ministry to undertake the suitable changes and inform the Committee about the
actions taken on these proposals as and when the changes have been introduced.

            The Committee strongly feels that traditional/indigenous games have not been given due attention as there appears
to be no scheme specifically for this purpose.  The Committee is of the opinion that the traditional/indigenous games need
not only be preserved but be also promoted in a planned manner.   The Committee disapproves this piecemeal approach in
this regard.  The Committee, therefore, emphasizes the need for a focussed policy to promote traditional indigenous
games.  It is of the opinion that Ministry should take all necessary steps urgently with a clear vision to achieve the goal.

            The Committee is of the opinion that the details of grants shown in the Table is self-revealing about the Ministry’s
attitude towards the traditional/indigenous sports.  The Committee is particularly perturbed over the quantum of assistance
for games like Kho-Kho and Kabaddi.  It recommends the Ministry to increase the financial assistance to these NSFs and
also to recognize more traditional/indigenous games.                                                                                                     (para
10.3)
XI
        ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
            The Committee notes that the Ministry has deliberately tried to be evasive in its reply.  It advises the Ministry to
give complete replies to a Parliamentary Committee.  The Committee would like to have names of the NSFs who have not
submitted their LTDPs and their annual calendar of events for the last three years.(para 11.6)
 
            Non-payment of outstanding dues by NSFs continues to be a serious matter.   The Committee appreciates that
outstanding dues against various federations has now come down to Rs. 2,24,80,300 from Rs. 4,40,37,520 in 2005.  Half
of the backlog still persists.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to take strict measures to liquidate the
outstanding dues against erring NSFs.  (para 11.7)      
             The Committee has not been informed about the pending utilization certificates of the central assistance given to
the NSFs.  The Ministry has informed that to ensure proper utilization of funds, the accounts and UCs of the previous
similar events are invariably obtained before considering fresh cases of grants.  Assistance is released based on the UCs,
audited accounts and performance report etc. of each event submitted by the NSF concerned.   The Committee is not
inclined to believe that there would be no pending UCs from various NSFs.   The Committee desires that the Ministry give
full details of the grants released and level of utilization by every NSFs getting financial assistance from the Ministry for
the last three years.                         (para 11.8)
 
            The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made so far in the special audit of various Federations
conducted by CAG.   The Committee would also appreciate if an idea about the follow-up action initiated in respect of
those Federations where CAG has given its Report, were provided to it.         (para 11.10)
 
XII       PROMOTION OF SPORTS AMONG DISABLED
 
            The Committee observes that only a token provision was made for the Scheme in 2004-05 and 2005-06, as the
Scheme had not been formulated.   The Scheme was proposed to be merged in the umbrella Scheme 'Scheme relating to
Events'.  Hence no allocation was made for 2006-07.  Separate provision for the Scheme during 2007-08 indicates that
again there is a change in the formulation of the Scheme.   The Committee observes that launching of this Schemes has

an appropriate policy/schematic framework in this regard is yet to be received.   The Committee strongly recommends the

            The Committee recommends the Ministry to formulate the estimates at the earliest so that there can be adequate
time to examine and allocate the funds.(para 13.1)
 
            The Committee finds an ad-hocism in projections and formulation of estimates for hosting an international event
like this.  It seems that there exists no clear schematic guidelines in this regard.  The Committee strongly recommends the
Ministry to come out with a clear guideline in this regard so that the expenditure on bid process and other necessary
expenditure can be met.      (para 13.5)
 
            The Committee is surprised to know that funds have been projected/allocated for every other activity such as
construction of games village, stadia, roads, transport, etc. but not for the training of our sportspersons for the
Commonwealth Games.  The Committee in one of its previous reports had proposed that some percentage of total
allocation for the games should be kept for training of our sportspersons.  The Committee is of the opinion that the
Ministry must create a special corpus for the training of athletes for the Commonwealth Games and other such events.  The
Committee hopes that the Ministry appreciates the high expectations the country has about its performance at the Games. 
The good showing will also bring a change in perception towards sports in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that every effort be made for a world-class training of our athletes on a regular basis.
                                         (para 13.6)
 
            The Committee notes that major works relating to the Games are yet to begin; these were expected, according to
the Ministry, to start from June-August, 2007.  The Committee expresses its apprehension about timely completion of
various stadia, games village and other facilities for this Game.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to start the civil

opportunity to familiarize themselves with facilities/equipment/grounds much in advance.

            The Committee observes that only a token provision of Rs. 1.00 lakh  has been made for 2007-08.  For a Scheme

Committee would like the Ministry to prepare a proper vision plan and establish these academies on sound footing.       
                                                            (para 14.2)

            The Committee strongly feels that the recommendations/observations of the Working Group are very relevant in
the present scenario.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that required action may be initiated at the earliest.(para
15.2)

            The Committee after going through the replies and other documents relating to Demands for Grants of various
years including that of 2007-08 arrives at conclusion that the financial performance/management of the Ministry leaves
much to be desired.  Importance of the mandate of the Ministry – development, empowerment of youth as well as
promotion of sports – can hardly be over-emphasized.  The Committee has all these years been pleading for more funds for
these purposes.  Rs. 200 crore for development of youth who constitute 45% of our population and on whom the country is
pinning all its hope for future, is just a peanut.   Similarly, sports development gets Rs. 350 crore + Rs. 150 crore for
Commonwealth Games, 2010.                                                                         (para 16.1)
 
            On the other hand, the Committee regrets to say that even these meagre allocations are not being utilized

completely and properly.  Every year, crores of rupees are left as unspent balance or being allowed to lapse due to various
reasons-non-settlement of accounts and pending UCs being the two most important ones.  As a result, crores of rupees are
blocked every year and our schemes languish.  Another disturbing trend noticed in this regard is the quantum jump in

3.7       Major Constraints
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.7.1    Several social, economic administrative and other reasons seem to act together as constraints to access and equity
in higher education.  Factors like rural-urban divide, gender disparity, regional imbalances, decreasing public allocation,
economic hardship, increasing cost due to commercialization, etc. are some of the major reasons of this phenomena. This
scenario of higher education, particularly in the ever-expanding competitive environment, does not inspire required
confidence, if India were to play its assigned role at the global level.   The Committee, therefore, believes that India has
to rise to the occasion urgently and make its higher education system not only competitive but also accessible and
affordable to everyone.
 
Action taken

sound fundamentals, good analytical abilities and appropriate utility-oriented skills are on rise and they are in great
demand. The Committee finds that most of our universities and colleges are providing out-dated, if not sub-standard
education in these disciplines, leading to the degrees and diplomas of little or no substance. The content as well as the

content and curriculum is carried out periodically. It has to be in keeping with indigenous conditions and requirements.

6.1       The Committee takes note on the fact that importance of management in education was underlined for the first
time in India by the National Policy on Education (NPE) in 1986.  The Policy called for evolving a long-term planning
and management perspective and its integration with the country’s developmental and manpower needs.  It emphasized
the need for making decentralization, autonomy for educational institutions and the principle of accountability the
guiding principles in remodeling the management of education.   The ‘Programme of Action’ for implementing the NPE
called for specific initiatives for the management in higher education.  Accordingly, a UGC Committee was established
to look into the matter and recommend on the pattern of management of universities.  The Committee was informed that
this UGC Committee stopped short of advocating any major overhaul of university, management.   The NIEPA, the
universities and the management institutes are also not known to offer any major programmes for educational
management.
 
Action taken
 
The observations have been noted. NIEPA has now been declared Deemed to be University with a broader mandate in
teaching and research in educational planning, administration and management.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.4       The Committee feels that it is high time that aspects like performance measurement, quality improvement,
professional development, institutional and cultural change, resource mobilization, marketing of the intellectual
products, public relations etc. are imbued in the practices of higher education management in our country.
 
Action taken
 
The UGC has evaluated the performance of the universities with respect to its performance in the areas of academic,
research and governance with the help of development radars.  Most of the parameters mentioned by the Hon’ble
Committee are used as indicators for evaluating the performance of the universities.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.5       The Committee believes that there is an urgent need to adopt best managerial practices in the structure of higher
education institutions and universities, since these are no longer traditional institutions engaged only in creation,
presentation and dissemination of knowledge. Rather they are progressively being called upon to involve themselves in a
variety of problems and concerns of national development, especially in the social and economic spheres.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendations have been noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.6       The Committee finds that there is no effective planning body in universities both central as well as State. The
Committee feels that it is only by better planning and optimum use of resources that universities can improve their
efficiency and can excel.   It is of the opinion that proper strategic planning keeping in view the priorities and options
available be adopted in the planning activities of the universities.
 
Action taken
 
Most of the universities have Academic Council and Executive Council which are involved in the effective planning of
the resources and courses of the universities.  Each university in terms of its autonomous status is free to device planning
mechanism.
 
Recommendations/Observations

6.7       The Committee is also of the view that autonomy to the universities be made inviolable because it is, the life-
breath to intellectual and academic initiatives and innovations. This autonomy, however, should not lead to autocracy
and it must be ensured that academic bodies were kept away from any kind of interference, political, bureaucratic and
any other views of academicians should have effective say in the management of higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.8       The Committee also recommends to ensure that academic decision in the institutions of higher learning is taken
on merit and the government control must be reduced. Any outside interference in appointments of university teachers
and administrators should be totally avoided. Direct interference of Finance Department in financial management of the
universities must also be avoided as it proves to be counterproductive.
 
Action taken
 
The Universities are given full autonomy in appointment of faculty position as per the norms laid by the UGC. There is
no outside interference in appointment, including from the Central Government.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.9       The Committee was informed that instances of uneasy relationship between various bodies, particularly the
Academic Council and the Executive Council in the universities are not very uncommon. This, the Committee feels,
prepares grounds for internal bickering and outside interference that ultimately vitiates the academic atmosphere in the
campuses. All possible measures be taken for avoiding such situations.
 
Action taken
 
The observations have been noted. These are the internal matters of the universities which can be best resolved by
adopting good governance measures by the                 Vice-Chancellors.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.10     The Committee is of the considered opinion that the role of a Vice-Chancellor in a university system is very
crucial. In today’s complex university environment, the person to be appointed as Vice-Chancellor must be the one who
is not only an academic leader but also trained in sound management practices. The Committee during its visit to IIM,
Ahmedabad came to know that the Institute was running an orientation programme for the CBSE school principals. The
Committee is of the opinion that all the IIMs may be requested to develop and run suitable modules for the orientation
and refresher courses for the Vice-Chancellors and Registrars of the universities as also for the heads of other institutions
of higher learning. The Committee also emphasizes the need for running such programmes in education management
specially designed for the government-officials responsible for implementing / supervising primary, secondary and
higher education.
 
Action taken
 
Highly eminent academicians are appointed as Vice-Chancellor. Any such programmes must not be imposed on them.  
A round table conference of all the newly selected Vice-Chancellors is conducted by the AIU from time to time to
familiarize them with techniques involved in professional management of higher education.
 
Recommendations/Observations

6.14     The Committee was informed that many a time, it has been experienced that University Acts in different States
have provision which are not longer relevant or are not keeping with the emerging challenges. The Committee
recommends that Ministry of Human Resource development should advise the State governments to review, from time
to time, their University Acts and amend them in the light of new requirements and challenged being faced by the
universities. UGC must take a lead in this exercise.
 
Action taken
 
The observations have been noted for following up with the states. Such issues also come under review during the
conferences of Chancellors of State Universities (Governors) with the President of India.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.15     The Committee is also of the opinion that for good governance, there is an urgent need for the use of
Management Information system in the universities. The Committee notes that majority of the universities have done it
in reference to examination & general administration. However academic governance has not been covered under this.
The Committee desires that academic governance be also brought in the Management Information System.
 
Action taken
 
Noted. Universities are encouraged to introduce management information system in the universities.   Universities have
also been provided V-SAT/Radio Link/Leased lines for connecting and a computer centre to enable them to adopt
computerized management information systems.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
6.16     The Committee is of considered view that system of micro-management be given up and structures of
governance outside universities also need reform. The Committee strongly feels that the internal management of
institutions needs to be strengthened. More autonomy and greater authority to the head of institutions may also be given.
There is a need to create a legal and conducive environment to initiate changes at the institutional level. It also needs to
be underlined that the government works as a facilitator rather than controller in the affairs of institutions of higher
learning.  
 
Action taken
 
The present policy of the Central Government is to encourage and protect autonomy of Institutions of higher learning.
 
VII.      Funding
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.1       The higher education system and the pattern of financing it, vary across the world, based on the size and strength
as well as degree of diversification of its institutions.  But the fact remains that they all face a severe constraint of public
finances available for higher education.  India is no exception in this regard.
 
Action taken
 
No comments are required.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.2       Funding of higher education in India has been an area of great concern because the resources are limited and
there is a need to balance the growing demands of higher education within the limited resources.  Of late, there has been
an intense debate over the pattern of funding education in general and higher education in particular. Public expenditure

196thReport of Human Resource Development

on education in India has increased significantly since the inception of planning in the country.  It has increased upto
more than Rs.9000 crores today.  The trend of public expenditure on higher education, the Committee notes, showed a
real rate of growth of 7.5% per annum during the 1950s, which went upto 11% during the 1960s.  In the following
decade, however, the annual growth rate came down to 3.4%, with only marginal recovery during the 1980s.  The public
expenditure per student, the Committee was informed, has also registered a negative growth in the 1990s.  The
Committee also notes that the share of higher education in Five Year Plans after increasing from 0.7% in the First Plan to
1.2% in the Fourth Plan.  It has ever since stagnated at 0.5% upto the Ninth Plan.  During Eighth Plan, it had further
come down to 0.3%.
 
Action taken
 
No comments are required.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.3       During the 1990s, the Committee observes, that the process of economic reforms and the concomitant structural
adjustments hit hard the expenditure on all social sector investments, including higher education.   With the general
withdrawal of subsidy and emphasis on cost-recovery, there has been a noticeable fall in the budgetary support to the
recurrent expenses.  This fall is visible not only in government contribution to higher education but also in the share of
higher education to the total expenditure on education.
 
Action taken
 
No comments are required.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.6       The Committee is of the view that the declining public finances for higher education coupled with the inflation
and increase in the number of students aspiring for it, severely impair its growth, both quantitative as well as qualitative. 
And this is what has happened in our country.  Reduction in expenditure on higher education, in fact, has affected not
only recruitment of the teachers and creation of physical infrastructure but has also restricted to a great deal access to
higher education particularly, by the poor people.  The Committee feels that for the economic and technological progress
of a country in this era of intense global competition, the country can ill-afford to ignore the higher education sector.  It
was argued before the Committee that lately, we have witnessed shifting of emphasis from higher education to primary
education.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that while universalizing primary education was the
constitutional mandate, the higher education also needs to be supported by increased allocations in the coming years,
should India were to provide higher education of world class standard.
 
Action taken
 
Observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.7       The Committee is aware of the resource constraints both with the Central and State Governments which cannot
fill the gap between the supply and demand of the higher education sector.  The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion
that new sources of financing higher education have to be found for bridging this gap.
 
Action taken
 
Observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations

7.9       In the light of this, the Committee feels that mobilizing resources from non-government sources has become
imperative now, not only to sustain the system of higher education at its present level but also for its further expansion
both in its qualitative as well as quantitative dimensions.
 
Action taken
 
This Ministry is of the opinion that increased public outlay in higher education cannot be overlooked.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.10     An estimate puts this demand at Rs.3,400 crores for the remaining period of 10
th Plan. Managing such a huge
sum is an uphill task. This can be achieved inter alia by promoting distance education, private participation and cost
recovery methods.  Besides, the universities need to recognize the importance of helping themselves through their
internal resource generation.  The Committee also feels that Income Tax concessions can be given to philanthropists and
to the community, should they invest in higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The CABE Committee on “Financing of Higher and Technical Education” has cautioned against increasing student fees,
revenues beyond a threshold, so that higher education remains affordable. Outlay on distance education has been
increased during 2006-07 and would continue to engage attention.
 
7.12     Student Fees
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.12.2  It was impressed upon the Committee that student fees were extremely low and had not been revised for
decades.  The Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five-Year Plan has also underlined the need for hike in the student fees. 
Some people advocated that fee could be one of the major sources of income in the present context.  It was argued by
them that currently, only about 15-20 percent of annual recurring cost per student was recovered from the students in the
form of fees, and remaining 80-85 percent came as subsidies from the government.
Action taken
 
There are limits to increase in student fees as revenue. Percentage of revenues of higher educational institutions cannot
be above a threshold level of 20 per cent, so that higher education is affordable.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.12.3  The Committee was also informed, on the other hand that fee income had been continuously on rise and it was
already on higher side and any further rise in it could cause much hardship to an ordinary household.
 
Action taken
 
No comments are required.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.12.4  The Committee is fully aware of the implications of hike in fee paid by students, as it may restrict the access to
the higher education. There is a possibility that beneficiaries, particularly from vulnerable groups, social and economic,
would find it difficult to afford the higher education affecting thereby their upward mobility adversely.   The Committee,
therefore, feels that raising of fee and other charges should be considered only after examining its social and economic
implications on the poor people.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should emphasize on
other options also. If the raise in the fee becomes unavoidable, it must be gradual and supplemented/supported by other
assistance.

Action taken
 
Observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
  
Recommendations/Observations
 
7.12.5  The Committee at the same time is of the opinion that it is not prudent to charge same fees from all students,
irrespective of their socio-economic status.  It is true that the daily pocket-expenses of some students are much more than
the fee they pay per month.  It is an anomaly.  Therefore, there is urgent need for having a rational and just policy in this
regard.  Meritorious students coming from weaker sections of the society need to be financially supported through
effective mechanisms so that their inability to afford the cost of education does not deprive them of higher education.
Therefore, provision of adequate and liberal free-ships and merit-cum-means scholarships to the students coming from
the disadvantaged groups is considered imperative.
 
7.12.6  What is a matter of concern to the Committee is the high fee structure of private colleges/universities.   The
Committee emphasizes that we must keep in mind the social and economic milieu of the students while deciding fee and
other charges.  The private institutions particularly unaided/self-financing colleges must ensure that education was not
made unaffordable to poor and meritorious student.  The Committee feels that a suitable formula for fixing/regulating
fees in private institutions of higher learning needs to be worked out in consultation and agreement with their
management.  The Committee notes that Courts have already suggested some mechanism in this regard.
 
Action taken (7.12.5 and 7.12.6)
 
A draft Central Bill for regulating fees in private unaided institution is pending finalization. The Ministry has announced
various scholarships scheme for the benefit of student community. Article 15(5) of the constitution enables the states to
make laws for the advancement of weaker section in matter of admission to all educational institutions including private
unaided professional educational institutions. Several States have enacted appropriate legislation for regulating fees by
private institutions.
 
7.14     Graduate/Exit Tax
 
Recommendations/observations
 
7.14.2  Imposition of Exit Tax on our students immigrating to other countries for taking up jobs after obtaining their
degrees, particularly from our premier institutions which are run on massive State subsidies, was suggested by some
experts who appeared before the Committee. They argued that the expenditure incurred on those students go without any
return to the country. The Committee would like to point out the changed perception about the traditional brain-drain
theory in the wake of globalization which recognizes certain indirect benefits - developing one’s skill further,
remittances in foreign exchange, etc. The Committee is of the view that students passing out from premier Government
institutions get the best education on payment of nominal fees. In the event of their leaving the country for good,
imposition of Exit Tax on them must be considered. The Committee, therefore, recommends that feasibility of this
proposal needs to be examined and implemented in the larger interest of the country.
 
 
Action taken
 
Noted for being conveyed to the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.

Recommendations/Observations
 
8.2       The Committee wonders that despite subsidized education and low fee structure, only about 7% of the students in

the age group of 18-23 years could afford to go to Universities and College. And those 83% who are left out, the
Committee feels, are not able to bear even that paltry fees.
 
Action taken
 
Access to higher education depends on both supply (capacity of institutions) as well as demand, which in turn is
determined by various factors including affordability.   Expansion in public investment as well as regulation of non-govt
provision are, therefore, unavoidable.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.3       The Committee understands that a high level of public subsidy reduces the scope for the government to mobilize
additional resources. It is also of the opinion that only the State can have long-term perspective and focus on social
concerns in promoting higher education. The State, therefore, cannot shy away from investing in higher education, as it
is a long-term investment for the overall economic development of the country and its people. Only State can invest in
basic research and development without any profit in financial terms. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that until
the private participation and the concerns associated with it were taken care of, necessary legal framework was put in
place and adequate safeguards were provided for protecting interest of vulnerable sections of out society, the government
must continue to provide necessary for the purpose. Any indiscriminate reduction in subsidies would leave the sector to
the vagaries of market forces. The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Planning Commission, Ministry of Finance and
Department to spare adequate funds for higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The Constitution (93
rd amendment) Act, 2005 requires and enables the States to make suitable Laws for safeguarding
and protecting the interests of the weaker sections of our Society. The Department is of the firm view that public
investment in higher education should be increased substantially. The outlay for the Higher Education is expected to be
enhanced for the 11 th Plan (2007-2012). As a matter of fact, the outlay was increased successively and substantially
during the last two years of the Xth Plan.
8.4       Private Universities
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.4.2    Such a situation created genuine and serious concern in the minds of the parents and the students. Government
and UGC also tried to intervene by issuing certain guidelines/ regulations for establishment and maintenance of standard
in these private universities. But these guidelines, the Committee notes could not have much impact and these
universities continued to function unregulated, offering sub-standard education for a heavy price. Ultimately, the matter
went to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court came out heavily against all the private universities established under
the Chattisgarh Act declaring them illegal as the clause of the Act providing for the establishment of private universities
was declared ultra wires. It is, however, important to note that the Supreme Court did not hold the establishment of
private universities per se illegal.
 
Action taken
A university can be established by an act of parliament or act of State legislature. There is no distinction under the
Constitution between public or private universities.   A university not funded by the State or Public exchequer is
generally called a Private University.
 
8.5       Unaided Professional Institutions
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.5.1    The Country in recent years has witnessed emergence of self-financed institutions offering various courses in
engineering, medical, management, etc. That is mainly run by trusts and societies. Lakhs of enthusiastic men and women
have taken admission in these institutions. For example, if we take only engineering colleges, there was an intake of

more than 4 lakh students in 2004-2005 in the self-financed technical institutions scattered in different parts of the
country. The administrative and management structure of these institutions, the Committee came to know, was archaic.
While some of them are doing extremely well, others do not have even the basic infrastructure for the courses being
offered by them. Most of these institutions, the Committee was informed, suffered from acute shortage of qualified
teachers, lack of required facilities for teaching & research, etc. Two main problems bedeviling them are their admission
procedure and the fee structure. Huge sums are charged for admission under different categories followed by hefty
tuition and other fees.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted. The shortage of qualified teachers is owing to the
competing demands of the other sectors of the economy. The Central Government is constantly endeavoring to ensure
that talented young persons are attracted to the teaching profession. Several long term measure, including a review of the
remuneration packages are required to be considered. In the short term, the AICTE permits reappointment of teachers
upto the age of 70 years in order to meet the shortages in unaided institutions, subject to capacity of persons thus
appointed. The admission procedure as well as the fee structure in unaided educational institutions are indeed cause for
alertness. The Constitutions (93
rd Amendment) Act, 2005 enables the Centre as well as State to make appropriate laws in
this regard in the interest of the weaker section. Several States have enacted laws for the purpose. A Central law is
pending finalization in this regard.  
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.5.3    While doing so, we must give due regard to views/concerns of the people opening these institutions. Otherwise,
good spirited people would feel discouraged to come forward in this regard.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.5.4    Steps should be taken to ensure that these institutions are properly assessed and accredited by the respective
agencies. Furthermore, the Private Institutions be rated by independent rating and their ratings be disseminated through
print and internet across the country. The Committee is of the considered view that such a publicly announced ratings
would help the students in selecting an institution to enroll in; the institutions in upgrading its standards; and the
employers in assessing the quality of graduating from these institutions. The Committee also desires that all such
educational institutions need to come to out with their Annual Reports containing necessary details about the courses
offered, quality of faculty, teaching, students strength, examination results, infrastructure and facilities available, the
corpus available and the source of funding, accreditation ratings, etc.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendations have been noted. The National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) an Inter-
University Centre under the UGC Act rates institutions which are affiliated to Universities or declared on deemed
universities. Statutory Councils such as the AICTE do prescribe and enforce standards in respect of curriculum. In
addition, the Association of Indian Universities (AIU) facilitates equivalence and mutual recognition of degrees among
its member. The web-site of the AICTE now gives all relevant information in respect of recognition institutions
including unaided institutions. Annual Reports of Deemed to be Universities are received by the UGC.

X.        Foreign Universities
 
 Recommendations/Observations
 
10.1     The Committee observes that with the sweeping economic and financial reforms set in motion by Government
of India since beginning of the nineties, nearly all sectors, including education has felt the impact in a big way. A large
number of foreign educational institutions have started establishing their presence in India.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
10.2     The Committee notes that the existing laws and regulations of the country do not provide any statutory
mechanism for regulating the operation of such foreign institutions in this country. It is only the AICTE that has come
up with a notification that carries revised regulations for the entry and operation of foreign universities/institutions
imparting technical education in India. The Committee is aware that the C.N.R.Rao Committee has been set up by the
Government for reviewing this aspect. The Committee only hopes that the Government would take necessary interim
measures in this regard before the Rao Committee’s recommendations are considered and accepted.
 
10.4     According to the information compiled by the Association of Indian Universities during the year 2000 on the

basis of advertisements appearing in the Indian newspapers, 144 foreign universities and colleges/institutions have been
offering various courses of study to the Indian students. Out of them, 117 offer programmes on their home campuses and

UK and Australian followed by USA and Canada and New Zealand. The remaining 14 institutions are from other

As mentioned earlier, the Government is in process of bringing in a legislation for regulation of entry and operations,

XI.       Deemed Universities
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Existing institutions may be given university status under a provision in the UGC Act which are known as Deemed
Universities. These institutions offer advance level courses in a particular field, while many of them award general
degrees. Currently, we have 95 deemed universities in different parts of the country. The Committee came to know
through several experts who appeared before it that the quality & standard in many deemed universities were seriously
wanting. It was also informed that the concept of deemed universities has not been able to achieve the desired objectives.
The Committee, therefore, feels that there is an urgent need for reviewing the procedure and criteria for providing
deemed university status to an institution.
 
Action taken
 
Deemed to be University status is granted to the institutions on the recommendations of the University Grants
Commission (UGC), as per the provision under Section 3 of the UGC Act 1956. Therefore, the recommendation was
referred to the UGC. Which has now informed that the Commission is seized of the matter of revising the guidelines for
processing the proposals from the institutions of higher learning seeking deemed to be university status.
 
XII.      State Universities
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
12.4     The Committee at the same time feels that we need not only more qualified but also highly motivated teachers. In
order to attract/retain them, we have to supplement their salaries with an attractive package of perquisites and support for
academic activities coupled with appropriate recognition with outstanding achievement.
 
Action taken
 
The salaries of the teachers of the universities/colleges are considered for enhancement    as and when the Central
Government enhances the salaries of its employees on the basis of recommendations of the Pay Commission. There are
incentives for teachers with Ph.D./M.Phil degrees and a Career Advancement Scheme (CAS) Scheme is also there for all

XIV     Role of the UGC
 
Recommendations/observations
 
14.2     The UGC was established to promote, coordinate and determine standards in respect of higher education in the
country. The Committee is of the opinion that the UGC has not been able to live upto the expectations. It has become
unequal to the task and challenges before it.  It is now functioning mainly as grant disbursing body than a body for the
promotion of teaching/research and maintenance of standards in higher education. The institutions of higher learning in
India have become just degree conferring bodies than academic and intellectual entity.
 
14.3     Today, something like 50 to 60 percent of our colleges do not have even the basic infrastructure, qualified
teachers, lab, libraries, etc. there has been no way of regulating the proliferation of such colleges. The Committee is
perturbed to see that after nearly 50 years of the UGC’s existence, there is no set of rules regulating the establishment of
substandard colleges. The Committee is of the opinion that the UGC should not act as Department of the government but
should act as a professionally body in which the university interests should be fully represented.
 
Action taken (14.2 and 14.3)
 
The UGC is discharging its duties in coordinating and determining, maintaining standards of teaching / research in
higher education. In addition the UGC is making all efforts to make Institutions of Higher Learning to function towards
academic excellence.  It is also monitoring various programmes through respective bureau and monitoring Cell. In order
to provide infrastructure facilities the UGC has established six Regional Offices and one NRCB. Through these offices,
the colleges which are recognized under section 2(f) and 12(b) Act of UGC are being provided grants for books and

provided fellowships to do their M.Phil/Ph.D degrees. Colleges are given grants to organize local state level, national
level and International level seminars. Teachers are provided minor research projects to inculcate research culture at
under graduate level.  
 
Recommendations/observations
 
14.10   It is suggested that full-time members of the UGC to look after different portfolios falling under higher education
be provided for and their numbers be increased in comparison to the present system, which permit for only a full-time
Vice-Chairman to assist the Chairman. Further, these members should chosen from the top three-four experts in a

The Chairman of UGC is not only assisted by the Vice Chairman but also by other members of the Commission as well

III.       ACCESS AND EQUITY
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.3       The Committee observes that higher education in India was never freely available to all; it was basically elitist in
nature due mainly to historical and other reasons. Even after its expansion in post-Independence period, it could not be
made a mass activity.   Even today, it is neither fully accessible nor equitous. The Committee is of the opinion that the
issues of access & equity, in fact, are the two core issues to the expansion of higher education and hence, to the overall
progress of a nation. The Committee, therefore, underlines the urgent need for broadening access to higher education by
expanding it and by making it affordable.
 
3.4       The Committee is of the view that the two issues of access and equity are inextricably linked to one another.
There are two aspects of issue of access. Firstly, it can be looked as percentage of our young people (18-23 years) who
are eligible for higher education. Only close to seven per cent of our young people in this age-group today are in higher
education. The corresponding figure in the OECD countries is as high as 45-50 per cent and is over 90 per cent in
countries like Canada.
 
 
 
Action taken (3.3 and 3.4)
 
Concerns of Equity in access to Higher Education had not been adequately addressed until recently. The Constitution
(93
rd Amendment) Act, 2005 enables the Centre as well as the States to further conditions for success in higher
education in a manner that the weaker sections are not excluded from access to higher and technical education.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee fails to understand the contention that the 93
rd Amendment alone could address the concerns of equity
and access to higher education. While this recommendation aimed at extending access to higher education to some
sections of the society, the Committee’s emphasis was for increasing access to all the sections of the society including
the weaker ones. The Committee would, therefore, like to have further comments of the Ministry on this aspect.

our remaining in global race as also for sustainable development of the country.

3.9       Regional Disparity
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.9.1    The Committee notes the conclusion of a study undertaken by a group of Indian scholars based in Japan and
USA, which had analyzed the funding of Higher education in different states by the Department. The study has shown
that Union Government’s expenditure on higher education to various states was grossly uneven. For example, last year’s
budget’s allocation for the states like Bihar, Rajasthan, Orissa, etc., was highly inadequate. Per person expenditure on
higher education in Bihar was Rs.1.87, in Rajasthan Rs.2.59 and in Orissa it was Rs.4.07 while in States like
Uttaranchal, it was Rs.105.42, in Arunachal Pradesh Rs.105 and in Assam Rs.77.7.
 
3.9.2    Another distinctive feature of regional disparity is visible in the number of colleges/institutions located in
different States. The four Southern States and Maharashtra having 32% of India’s population have 46% of total general
colleges and almost 60% of professional institutions. In contrast, in the States of UP, MP and Bihar (including
Jharkhand) having 34% of population, only 23% of general colleges and only 14% of professional colleges are located.
The Committee is concerned to see that in the most populous States where nearly ¾
th of our population lived, the access
ratio is far below the national average. It presents quite a dismal picture about the existing status of higher education in
the country.
 
3.9.3    The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need to remove this regional disparity.   It is high time that
Central Government takes some initiatives for encouraging and helping the State Governments to set up educational
institutions in tune with the global requirements.
 
Action taken (3.9.1 to 3.9.3)
 
While the Central Government is not aware of the authenticity of the said study mentioned by the Hon. Committee, it
may be mentioned that the Central Governments’ expenditure on higher education is mainly in respect of development
and maintenance of Central Educational Institutions (Central Universities, IITs, etc.) and the Central Government

dependent on State Govts for development   and maintenance.   Therefore, States with no or fewer Central Institutions
would, obviously, have lower per person public expenditure from the Union Budget. This situation can be remedied only
with more public outlay and expansion of Central Institutions.  Recent initiatives of the Central Government e.g. in

observations of the Hon’ble Committee would be taken into serious consideration in the strategies for the XIth Plan.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee notes that the MHRD has not given satisfactory reply to this recommendation. The Ministry has
subsequently informed the Committee about several strategic interventions that have been proposed in the XIth Plan.
The Committee would like to know about the interventions that have finally been included in the XIth Plan. The
Committee also observes that 12 large States not having adequate technical institutions have been approached for taking
corrective steps. Response from these States is awaited. The Committee is of the view that such an initiative followed by
persuasive approach is bound to bear fruit. The Committee would like to be apprised in this regard. 
 
3.10
          SCs/STs in Higher Education
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
The Committee notes that the UGC had tried to help the under-privileged sections of the society through some special
schemes. A Remedial Coaching scheme for the benefit of students belonging to the SC/ST and weaker sections of the
society was introduced in 1994.  Another scheme of remedial coaching was introduced with a view to improve the
overall performance of these students in the examinations. The Commission introduced the scheme of establishment of
SC/ST cells in the universities in the year 1983, with a view to provide information regarding facilities available for
SC/ST students in universities and colleges. The SC/ST Cells are closely monitoring the implementation of reservation
policy in higher education. But these attempts, the Committee notes have not helped much.  For example, the enrolment
of SCs in higher education has ranged between 8.6 per cent in 1990-91 to 11.3 per cent in 2002-03. Enrolment of ST
students in higher education was between 2.1 per cent to 3.6 per cent in 1990-91 and 2003-04 respectively.   The
Committee recommends that special programmes for encouraging students from backward and minority communities
also need to be prepared urgently as their participation in higher education is abysmally low, as compared to their
percentage in total population. This poor situation reflects the poor enrolment and retention of all children including the
SC/ST students in school education. All efforts be made to ensure the enrolment and retention of students right from
school level.
 
Action taken
 
The objectives of the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan aim to improve enrolment and retention, which in turn would generate
greater demand from among the weaker sections for higher education.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The reply of the MHRD is not upto the mark. The Committee feels that the existing UGC schemes are meant only for
those who have reached the higher education level. There appears to be no serious effort being made for bringing more
and more students from these categories to the universities. The Committee would, therefore, like to have a more
specific reply in this regard. The Committee is also of the view that there is a need for giving wide publicity to the

3.11
          Convergence of Conventional and Distance Mode
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
The problem of access and equity is closely linked to opportunity. The Committee feels that the solution to the problem
of opportunity lies in convergence of conventional with modern distance education systems with open and flexible
structure. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion that we must exploit our ICT potential for its
penetration to the country’s remotest corners to expand the access to higher education.   The Committee is of the view
that the Government should make an earnest beginning to train the people for utilizing the latest technologies to make
the higher education easily accessible. It would also cut across the rural-urban divide as well as gender disparities in this
regard.
 
Action taken
 
The ICT potential of the EDUSAT is being harnessed by institutions such as Consortium for Educational
Communication (CEC), an Inter University Centre of UGC, EMRCs, the IGNOU, the AICTE, the NECERT, the IITS
and others including several State Universities.   The UGC would work towards further convergence of the different
modes of higher education. A one-stop Education Portal is also being developed with a view to expanding access and
improving quality of learning at various stages of education.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is informed that the EDUSAT capacity is not being utilized to the optimum level and many educational
institutions are not taking advantage of the technology. This needs to be looked into and the MHRD has to devise
adequate strategies and create facilities, technical or otherwise, to enable educational institutions to take advantage of the
facility.
 
3.12
          System of affiliation
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Another issue that Committee wishes to highlight is about system of affiliation.   In India most of its 16000 odd colleges
are affiliated ones. In the absence of proper facilities, many of these colleges perform only classroom teaching in a
traditional way. The Committee was informed that nearly 89 per cent of UG students, 66 per cent of PG students and 85
per cent of the faculty in higher educational institutions, were in these affiliated colleges. Consequently, the M.Sc., MA,
Ph.Ds that are coming out of such colleges are undoubtedly of poor quality. What is worse, in India major affiliating
universities are over-burdened with the administrative works which are unproductive in academic terms. The Committee
is of the view that this certainly telling upon the academic competence of our universities. The VCs of such universities
are left with no time for their academic pursuits. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be a cap on
the number of colleges being affiliated to a university. For this, we would need to open more and more universities for
which about 1000 universities and university level institutions be set up by 2015 in the Central, State and private sector.
A country like Japan, it may be noted, has around 700 universities and USA has nearly 3000 of them. Besides, setting up
more universities, we must encourage good colleges and institutions to acquire ‘deemed university’ or autonomous status
by fulfilling the norms laid down in this regard. This, the Committee feels, would not only lessen the burden of
universities but also enhance their quality and output greatly. Besides, the colleges should be encouraged to offer more
and more applied courses by offering job-oriented courses particularly after 10+2. These measures, if taken up in a
planned and fixed schedule would go a long way in decreasing the unnecessary burden on our universities.

3.14     Distance Education Council
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.14.1  The Distance Education Council (DEC) has been created under the IGNOU Act for the promotion and
coordination of Open University and distance education system and for the determination of its standard. The Committee
found that the opinion is divided on the power of the DEC to recognize/approve the courses/degrees being offered by the
various other universities/institutions in the country by distance mode. It is argued that the DEC having been created
under the Act of a university should not have such jurisdiction in respect of courses/degrees offered by the other
universities. It may be pointed that the DEC has been issuing notifications to universities asking them to get their
programmes approved quoting a particular Gazette Notification regarding students not being eligible for Central
Government jobs, if they pursue courses not approved by the DEC. Many of the universities are not prepared to accept

education. Information given by the Department to the Committee was simply taken out of UGC Annual Report 2004-

exact status of women in higher education. So much so, the allocations and expenditure made for the women-specific
programmes, which form a part of gender-budgeting that every Department has to have, was conspicuous by absence in

The Gender Budgeting Cell is functional at present. In regard to the references to the UGC Annual Report, it may be

Therefore, the government has to depend on the UGC for authenticated information.

As regards the allocations and expenditures made for women specific schemes/programmes, the Committee hopes that
the newly created Gender Budgeting Cell would project only those allocations and expenditures which were exclusively

Recommendations/observations
 
3.15.8  The UGC scheme for opening women study centres in the universities, the Committee found, could not pick up
and precious little appears to have been done in this regard. The Committee recommends that it must be ensured that all

The UGC set up Women’s studies Centre in 72 Universities and a total grant of Rs.779.80 lakhs has been released to the

Centres.

The Committee is not at all happy with the scheme of Women Study Centres as it has never taken off properly. Of the
357 odd universities and equivalent institutions in the country, only 72 of them have Women Study Centres today. The
Committee is further informed that as many as 104 proposals were pending with the UGC and that these will be
considered only in the XIth Plan, as recommended by a Standing Committee of UGC constituted to review the Scheme.
The information provided to the Committee is sketchy and does not give a very clear picture of the recent developments
in the matter. The Committee would, therefore, like the Ministry to submit a detailed note in this regard.
 
IV.       Relevance
 
Recommendations/observations
 
4.1      Education be it primary, Secondary or higher, if it is not contextual and relevant will not be able to meet the

challenges and demands of the time. It notes that in today’s world, thing in every walk of life are changing at a very
fast pace. It has, therefore, become a daunting task for education to keep pace with the challenges posed by the
contemporary socio-economic transformation. Higher education, in fact, faces this impact more than other levels.
Relevance of higher education, therefore, becomes of utmost significance for the development and survival of a
nation in the changes global/liberal context. In the Committee’s view, its relevance should be seen with reference to
marketability of the graduate and postgraduate students it produces; with reference to its reach to marginalized
sections; and its relevance for the socio-economic development of a society.

No comments are required.

The Committee is not happy with the response of the Ministry; it should have responded to by making specific

4.3       Vocational Education
 
Recommendations/observations
 
4.3.1   The Committee notes that as envisaged in the National Policy on Education as also in the revised Plan of Action-
1992, the UGC implemented the recommendations made by the Core Committee on Vocationalisation (Career
Orientation) of Education.  This was to ensure that the students at the first degree level develop knowledge, skills and
attitudes for gainful employment with emphasis on self-employment. Since 1994-95, a large number of colleges and
universities, the Committee was informed, had been identified to provide assistance under the scheme on selective basis.
The Committee was informed that the UGC, in fact, had been receiving very good response from the
universities/colleges to start vocational courses in various subjects, but not all such requests from the
universities/colleges could be agreed to because of the inadequacy of funds. This, according to the Committee, indicates
that the students are accepting the concept of Vocationalisation of Education as it is job-oriented and a move towards
entrepreneurship. The Committee, therefore, recommends that inadequacy of funds should not act as an obstacle to
vocationalisation of education. It would, in fact, reduce the undesired pressure on universities and institutions of higher
learning. Adequate funds be allocated for this purpose.
 
Action Taken
 
Enhanced Plan allocation of Rs.1269.80 crores has been made to UGC during 2006-07 as against Rs.786.30 crores in
