Comments of the Committee
 
It appears that the UGC does not have any effective and comprehensive scheme for promoting vocational education in a
big way. The Committee would appreciate if the Department takes up this issue with the UGC. The fund allocation for
this purpose is inadequate that needs to be considerably increased.
 
Recommendations/observations
 
4.3.2   The scheme of vocationalisation of education actually, stipulates a close coordination between the industries and
educational institutions. The institutions intending to avail of the scheme of Vocationalisation of Education and
applying to the UGC for financial assistance, are required to submit a letter of intent to UGC duly signed by the
industries that the students will have on-the-job training and other practical experiences in their industries and that they
will pick up some of the students after completion of particular vocational course. The Committee is of the opinion that

linking of education with industry is something very desirable today. The Committee believes that industry-institution

with industries, Committee believes, would encourage more and more students to opt for the vocational streams instead

The Committee believes that existing linkage between industry and academia leaves much to be desired. A close relation

4.4.      Dual Degree
 
Recommendations/observations
 
The Committee was informed that the UGC had allowed the system of earning certificate/diploma in utility-oriented
programmes through parallel mode alongwith the regular degree. This is to provide an alternative to the students just in
case. The AICTE has also allowed the system of earning dual degrees simultaneously. The Committee welcomes this
and feels that the system of degree plus certificate/diploma in utility oriented programme appears to be quite germane to
the emerging scenario where demand for skilled manpower in different disciplines is increasing at the global level. The
Committee feels that our ultimate objective should be to ensure that students do not merely have to look for a job;
instead they are able to create jobs for themselves and many others. Need of the hour, according to the Committee, is to
develop in-house faculty and other facilities in the colleges for this purpose. This will make our colleges more vibrant
and attractive. This is an area, the Committee feels, where public-private partnership can play a creative role in
augmenting the activities of our colleges. The Committee at the same time expresses its apprehension about the
possibility of main degree neglected at the cost of utility-oriented one, as a result, a student may not be able to show his
best in either. This aspect needs to be taken care of by the UGC and AICTE.  We must also put a system of accreditation
for such courses.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendations have been conveyed to the UGC and the AICTE. 
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee has learnt that the UGC has constituted an Expert Committee to assess the impact of dual degree on the
main programme. It would like to be apprised of the latest in this regard.
 
The Committee would also like the Ministry to specifically respond to the recommendation of putting in place a system
of accreditation for dual courses. 
 
4.5       Promoting Research
 
Recommendations/observations
 
4.5.3    Lack of allocation from state kitty is also a reason for poor research activities in the universities. The Committee

4.5.4. On further questioning, the Committee was informed about some schemes run by UGC and also about the

5.         Quality and Excellence
 
Recommendations/observations
 
5.8       The Committee feels that there is a need for instilling a sense of accountability in teaching community. The
Committee found that the quality of many teachers, if not all, does not inspire confidence as scholars; or researchers or
as educationists. The Committee recommends to carry out some kind of performance-audit of the teachers and in this
process, the students’ participation must also be ensured. The Committee strongly feels that the conditions of service,
remuneration and career advancement of the teachers be linked with their overall performance.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of Hon’ble Committee have been noted.   
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee has been informed that the issue of student’s involvement in performance audit of teachers is a matter
which requires taking into account the response of the academic community before it could be considered for
implementation. It is further learnt that the MHRD is of the view that universities enjoy autonomy in academic matters
and hence suggestions of appraisal of performance of teachers should be left to the discretion of each university to adopt,
as it deems appropriate. The Committee also appreciates the importance of autonomy of the universities. It, however,
believes that no performance audit of the teachers would be complete without student’s participation. The Committee,
therefore, reiterates its recommendation in the matter.
 
Recommendations/observations
 
5.9       The Committee is of the opinion that examination reforms be carried out so that “learning by rote” is replaced by
“learning for joy”. The Committee strongly feels that semester system should be introduced instead of the one-time final
examination. The advantage of the semester system is that assessment of student performance becomes a continuous and
integral part of the teaching-learning process. Also, a mechanism for joint conferring of degree by the university as well
as colleges concerned will make colleges more responsible as their name will also appear on the degree.

According to the UGC, a large number of institutions have been switching over to semester mode of examination vis-à-
vis the conventional mode of annual examination for assessment of student performance. Such a reformative measure

Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is informed that a system of joint conferring of degrees as contained in para 5.9 is operational. A note

5.10     Assessment & Accreditation
 
Recommendations/observations
 
5.10.1  The National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) was established by the UGC in 1994 to assess the
quality and accredit universities and colleges depending upon certain specified parameters/indicators. The Committee
was however, informed that even after almost two decades, the process of assessment and accreditation has not had the
desired impact. Hardly 10 to 15% of the total higher & technical education institutions have gone through this process
mainly due to inadequate infrastructure and other weaknesses in the NAAC.
 
5.10.2  A major weakness in the existing institutional assessment, the Committee notes, is that while it assesses the
performance of the university or colleges as a whole; it does not do it Department-wise. What is known to the people is
the grades and stars, which signify only averages. Academic performance of a university, in fact, is mostly department-
specific. As a result, weaker ones are not exposed. Therefore, the idea of grouping them together for assessment, the
Committee feels, needs to be reconsidered. The Committee recommends that the NAAC should start accrediting
individual departments also of a university in addition to its overall grading, at the earliest.
 
5.10.3  The Committee was informed that accreditation being voluntary, many institutions that have secured
accreditation may not turn up for re-accreditation after five years and may still continue to use the grade obtained earlier.
Others do not turn up for accreditation at all. The Committee is aware that it would be difficult to enforce, if
accreditation is made mandatory. The Committee proposes, as incentive for this purpose, that the accreditation must be
linked with the grants or special assistance/recognition by the UGC and other bodies so that institutions turn up for
accreditation. In USA, the Committee learnt, federal grants are available only to the accredited institutions.
 
5.10.4  The Committee was informed that the process and procedure of assessment and accreditation by the NAAC takes
a long time. It, therefore, emphasizes the urgent needs to identify efficient ways and effective strategies for expediting
the assessment and accreditation by NAAC within a stipulated time frame.
 
5.10.5  The Committee learnt that parameters adopted by the NAAC for evaluating the quality, although useful, leave
some scope for subjectivity in this exercise. The Committee recommends that this aspect should be re-examined with a
view to making these parameters transparent and objective.
 
5.10.6  The Committee also underlines the greater need for evolving an internal self-regulatory quality assurance
mechanism by the accredited institutions for maintaining and upgrading their quality level. This mechanism may also
monitor both academic excellence as well as administrative efficiency of that institution. Periodic assessment of
accredited institution should also be carried out regularly by the NAAC.
 
5.10.7  The Committee, in view of the emerging scenario, is of the opinion that a Government agency like NAAC for
assessment of standards and accreditation of higher educational institutions may not have the desired
credibility/acceptability to our higher education institutions at the international level. In fact, the need for a third party
evaluation model with participation of all the stakeholders in higher education was underlined by some experts who
appeared before the Committee. The Committee also feels that the establishment of an independent accreditation agency
having regional offices in different areas of the country should also be considered. The industry should also have its

196thReport of Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/196threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:40]
participation in such a machinery. It should be, more or less, on the lines of quality assurance bodies like ISO and other
rating agencies like CRISIL and ICRA.
 
Action taken (5.10.1 to 5.10.7)
 
The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are noted. There is an urgent need for giving a new orientation and
thrust to the functioning of NAAC so that it could meet the emerging challenges in the higher education system. Keeping
this in view, the Government had recently constituted a three-member Expert Committee to review the functioning of
NAAC. The said Committee has since submitted its report to the Ministry and some of the suggestions made by the said
Committee largely address the concern expressed by the Hon’ble Committee. In order to develop a credible, acceptable
and transparent accreditation process, the Experts have recommended identification of quality parameters and conversion
of scores obtained individually by the institution for each parameter, for computing overall grading of the institution, be
done with great care and clarity. The NAAC has attempted to modify the instrument of assessment with introduction of
key indicators. It has also modified the peer teams selection process which are now selected by computerized random
selection process from a panel approved by a Sub-Committee of the Executive Council of NAAC. Further, a series of
training programmes are also being organized by NAAC to minimize the scope for subjective peer judgment. The
NAAC has been advocating in-house mechanism called Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC) to be established in all
accredited institutions and the same has been made mandatory requirement for the institutions opting for re-
accreditation. The report of the Expert Committee also envisages continuation of active post accreditation process to
maintain certain standards for the institutions. The recommendations of the Expert Committee are presently under
consideration of the Government. 
 
Comments of the Committee (5.10.1 to 5.10.7)
 
The Committee is informed that the MHRD had constituted an Expert Committee to review the functioning of the
National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC). The recommendations of the Committee have been accepted
and the UGC has been advised to initiate necessary follow-up action on the recommendations in a time bound manner.
The Committee would like to have a brief status note about these recommendations and the action taken by the UGC.

          National Board of Accreditation

6.         Governance and Management
 
Recommendations/observations
 
6.2       With major interventions by the State for universalisation of education, latest being the SSA and MDM, the
Committee feels, the secondary and then the higher secondary education is bound to face in the coming years
unprecedented pressure of numbers as well as quality. Besides, the emerging new regime under GATS has also posed
newer challenges before higher education. Such a situation calls for a modern system of management for the higher
education to enable India to compete and survive at the global level. The Committee feels that our universities and
institutions of higher learning should be prepared to respond to such demands and challenges, and this cannot be done
without making suitable changes in the system of governance and administrative structures of higher education in the
country.
 
Action taken
 
Observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is not at all satisfied with the reply of the MHRD. It would like to know as to what specific steps are
being taken to meet the challenges before higher education today. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the
changes made/being made in the system of governance and administrative structures of higher education in the country.
 
Recommendations/observations
 
6.3       The Committee notes that management in education though not unknown in India, works more or less, on old
structure and concepts. It is a matter of concern that most of our universities have become merely examination boards for
conducting examinations and conferring degrees, apart from the major work of granting affiliations. The Committee is
dismayed to note that research as well as pedagogical innovations seems to have taken a back seat in the universities.
The Committee is of the considered opinion that in such a scenario what is needed is the greater autonomy,
professionalism, transparency and accountability in the administration of higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The current policy of the government is to encourage autonomy of institutions of higher learning.  
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is of the considered opinion that encouraging autonomy of institutions of higher learning alone may not
suffice. The MHRD has to evolve a more relevant system based on modern management techniques whereby
professionalism, transparency and accountability in the administration of higher education could be ensured.
 
Recommendations/observations
 
6.11     The Committee takes note of the fact that there are a number of regulatory bodies like the UGC, ICAR, AICTE,
MCI, NCTE concerning various areas of higher education. These bodies fall under different Ministries/Departments. It
was argued before the Committee that the existence of various regulatory bodies not only makes the system complex, but
also gives it a fragmented character. The Committee therefore, recommends that some kind of coordinating mechanism
at the national level be put in place in the best interest of efficiency and effectiveness. A board of Higher education at
National level for the purpose as visualized by the NPE 1986, could not be set up so far, for the reasons not known to the
Committee. The Committee recommends that the Union Ministry of Human Resource Development initiate and
coordinate with other Ministries like Agriculture, Health, Law and Finance to create a National Apex body for
coordination among the various regulatory agencies.

Recommendations/observations
 
7.4       The Committee was informed that the Central Government expenditure on higher education in real terms had, in

The reply of the Department is not relevant and fails to attend to the specific queries raised by the Committee in its
recommendation. The Committee is aware that a number of career-oriented courses are being offered by the universities
and colleges. What is, however, disturbing is that no survey has ever been conducted to assess their viability or the
absorption of the students undergoing these courses in industry or in other employments. In the absence of any such
surveys, it may not be long before these courses lost their relevance and became obsolete. Committee’s apprehension is
based on the data about various career-oriented programmes offered by universities/colleges under Arts/Social Sciences,
Commerce and Science offered during 2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-07. The Committee has observed variation,
both upward and downward, not only in the number of courses but also in the trend of either new subjects being
introduced or some subjects being withdrawn during this period. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
assessments of the courses may be carried out at regular intervals to ensure that they retain their relevance and meaning

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in
its One Hundred Eighty-third Report on Major Issues concerning Kendriya Vidyalayas of the Department of School
Education & Literacy.  The Committee had presented the Hundred and Sixty-second Report, a detailed analysis of various
aspects concerning the functioning of Kendriya Vidyalayas, to the Parliament on the 28

II.         NORMS FOR OPENING OF KENDRIYA VIDYALAYAS
 
Recommendations/Observation
2.1       Opening of Kendriya Vidyalayas is based on specific norms prescribed for this purpose by the Govt.  One of those
was the provision of 15 acres of land to be provided free of cost by the sponsoring agencies.  The Committee was informed
that this criterion had now been drastically reduced to 4.00 acres in a metropolitan city; a contiguous plot fairly leveled
measuring 6.00 acres in hilly terrain; 8.00 acres in urban area; and 10.00 acres in rural/semi urban area.  The Committee
appreciates that in view of the ever-increasing shortage of land in the present scenario, lowering the land requirement is
the need of the hour.  However, the Committee would like to emphasize that there should be no deviation from the need to
demarcate 40% as building area and 60% as play field of the 4.00 acres provided in a metropolitan city.
 
Action Taken
As suggested by the Committee due consideration is being given by KVS to demarcate 40% of the land for
building area and 60% as play field.
 
IV.       KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA BUILDINGS
Recommendations/Observations
4.3       The Committee observes that considerable time is taken in the various stages of construction including the delay,
sometimes, at the planning stage. What is more disturbing is that a large number of these KVs, has been opened way back
in eighties. The Committee understands that after a protracted procedure involving States/sponsoring agencies and
overcoming a number of hurdles, these KVs must have reached the stage when finally construction project could be
sanctioned. However, it appears that series of other procedural formalities are yet to be fulfilled, before the students could
pursue their studies in a proper environment having required infrastructure.
 
Recommendations/Observations
4.4       The Committee found that construction of another 28 school buildings was at the planning stage. The Committee
finds that these KVs are scattered in different State of the country, having various sponsoring agencies. The Committee is
concerned to note that out of these 28 KVs, no progress is expectedin 19 KVs, due to various reasons beyond the control
of KV Sangathan. In some cases construction agencies have not submitted even preliminary drawings and estimates. They
are reminded from time to time to expedite it. In such a situation the Committee is constrained to conclude that the
construction status of these KVs would continue to remain at the same stage. It appears that no agency is responsible and
KV Sangathan itself seems to have abdicated its responsibility/duty.
 
Action Taken
(4.3 & 4.4)
KVS works are being executed  through Govt. construction agencies as a “Deposit Work”, in which construction
agencies are responsible for planning, designing and execution of work as per their execution system of public work.
KVS’s role is to monitor the progress and release funds accordingly. In case of any hurdle and delay, KVS takes up the
matter with the Heads/site staff of concerned construction agencies. For proper and effective monitoring, review

the progress and other related problems.
(ii)        Review of works by Commissioner, KVS, with the Head of construction agency.
(iii)       Monthly review meetings at KVS level.
(iv)       Monitoring at Region level.
(v)        Monitoring at Vidyalaya level by Vidyalaya Monitoring Committee.
After transfer of suitable plot of land to a KV, construction works are entrusted to the Govt. construction agencies
and these are chased up regularly for submitting the drawings & estimate for issuing Admn. Approval and Exp. Sanction.
After the sanction is issued, Construction agency is regularly chased for early start of work by completing pre-tender
planning in time. On account of close monitoring as many as 32 school buildings have been got completed during this
period.
 
Recommendations/Observations
4.5       The Committee made an attempt to understand the factors primarily responsible for such a dismal situation with a
view to find a solution to break this impasse. The Committee summoned the DG, CPWD to discuss this problem as also to
understand his constraints. The Committee was given to understand that KV Sangathan has a well laid-out monitoring
mechanism functioning at different levels. The Committee, however, feels that this monitoring mechanism has not proved
to be very effective so far. The Committee observes that an initiative has been taken to simplify procedural formalities.
Henceforth, all sanction orders issued by KVS are to be forwarded to the concerned CPWD authorities by name. This
would result in eliminating undue delay occurring at various levels in KVS as well as in CPWD.
Action Taken
As regards, issuing of sanction order are concerned these are already being forwarded to the Heads of concerned
construction agency. However it is noted for compliance that in future all sanction orders will be issued by name to the
concerned authorities of CPWD.
 
Recommendations/Observations
4.6       Another problem noticed by the Committee was lack of co-ordination between the civil and electrical wings of
CPWD. This also, the Committee found, leads to unnecessary delays in this regards. The Committee is happy to note that
CPWD has since introduced a composite tendering system, where under electrical works inside the building are to be made
part of the main contract.
 
Action Taken
In the sanction order of school building project, KVS has already incorporated a clause of executing the work
through a composite tender.

Recommendations/Observations
2.2       The Committee came to know that out of 931 KVs in the country, there are 38 KVs where land had not been
provided by the sponsoring agencies even after several years, which in some cases is more than 20 to 25 years.  In the case
of as many as 27 KVs, sponsoring agencies were the Armed Forces.  The Committee notes that with the exception of two
KVs opened in the year, 2005-06, rest were opened between 1977-78 to 1997-98.  In the remaining 11 KVs also the
situation was, more or less, the same; the earliest KV was opened in 1973-74.  Details of such KVs reveal a very
discouraging picture.   The Committee hopes that with the revision of land norms, situation would improve.  The
Committee would like the Department of Secondary & Higher Education and KVS to vigorously pursue the allotment of
land with the concerned agencies and report the progress made in this regard to the Committee within three months.
 
Action Taken
Following efforts have been made to obtain land from the sponsoring agencies:

Comments of the Committee
The Committee had identified 38 Kendriya Vidyalayas where land had not been made available by the sponsoring
agencies even after a lapse of 20-25 years in some cases.  The latest status report in respect of these 38 Kendriya
Vidyalayas reveals that position remains unchanged.  Correspondence/meetings at different levels with all concerned have
not yielded any desired results.  The Committee observes that in most of the cases although land had been finally
earmarked by the sponsors, approval of the Ministry of  Defence / concerned State Government was awaited. The
Committee had called for a status report on this within three months.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that
it is already more than six months since the presentation of its report, but there is no indication of any noticeable progress. 
The Committee takes a serious view of this.  The Committee is of the firm view that it is high time that the matter is taken
up at the highest level, be it the Ministry of Defence or any State Government.
The Committee observes that land is to be provided in respect of total 126 KVs.  38 KVs pointed out by the

time-bound manner.
 
Recommendations/Observations
2.3       Besides the provision of land, the other basic criteria for opening a new KV is the availability of 200 children (500
in big cities) and minimum concentration of 1000 Central Government employees. In all the cases, proposal has to
emanate from State Government/Departments/Ministries/Defence authorities/PSUs.  Committee’s attention has been
drawn towards the opening of 98 KVs in a short span of two  years, i.e. during 2003-2004 and 2004-2005.  On a specific
query in this regard, the Committee was informed that only three KVs - two in the project sector and another one in Tehran
were opened on specific requests/proposals.  As regards the remaining 95, the Committee noticed a very disturbing aspect. 
In the normal course, demands for opening of a new KVs come from various sources, ranging from the elected
representatives to the State/project authorities.   However, the Committee was informed that these 95 KVs were opened
without there being a formal proposal from the KV Sangathan. These KVs were opened on communications received from
the then Chairman, KV Sangathan at different points of time. Opening of these KVs was apparently justified by the
availability of surplus teachers and need for utilizing their services.  The Committee was given to understand that ex-post
facto approval was proposed to be obtained from the Cabinet after the matter was discussed and approved in EFC
meeting.  That could, however, not be done.
 
Recommendations/Observations
2.4       The Committee takes a serious view of this development because the prescribed pre-sanction procedure for the
purpose was simply given a go by in these cases.  The Committee is perturbed to note that these 95 KVs were opened
without taking any prior approval/sanction.   Even the ex-post facto approval could not be taken.   The committee is not
happy with such an approach of short circuiting the established procedures.  In this case, in the absence of any formal
approval and their being no fund allocation specifically for these KVs plan funds are utilised to fulfill the salary and other
requirements of staff members, of these KVs.  This is not a healthy fiscal practice.

III.       PROJECT VIDYALAYAS
Recommendations/Observations
3.1       Committee’s attention was drawn towards the closure of a large number of project Vidyalayas due to failure of the
sponsoring agencies in providing the required funds.  The Committee reiterates that the Department and KVS should
approach the project authorities for re-opening of closed Vidyalayas.   Those Project Vidyalayas which could not be
revived may be taken over by the Government and run as normal KVs.
 
Action Taken
Budgetary allocations are given to KVS by the Ministry to manage the affairs of KVs which are opened with its
approval in the civil/defence sector. KVS is not given any funds from the Government to run Project Sector Vidyalayas.
Hence, the Project Authorities are expected to make available the required funds to re-open the KVs under Project Sector.
 
Comments of the Committee    
The Committee feels that the Department has not given much thought on the recommendations of the Committee
that those project vidyalayas which could not be revived may be taken over by the Government and run as normal
Kendriya Vidyalayas.  The Committee reiterates that the Department should approach the project authorities for reopening
of closed Vidyalayas.  At the sametime, wherever feasible, the Department should explore the possibility of taking over
those closed KVs which cannot be revived.  Basic idea behind this observation of the Committee was to make optimum
and judicious utilization of existing infrastructure/ facilities at these closed project Vidyalayas for the ultimate benefit of
our students.    
 
Recommendations/Observations
3.2       The Committee notes that there are 129 project sector KVs functioning at present. Outstanding dues amounting to
Rs.16.08 crore are to be paid by the sponsoring agencies. These dues may be against both closed as well as running project
sector vidyalayas. The Committee understands that the Ministry is pursuing with the concerned agencies for payment of
dues/pending against them. However, these efforts seems to have failed, as only three PSUs have responded and these too
have expressed their inability in liquidating their dues. The Committee finds the situation quite discouraging. The
Committee is of the view that this matter needs to be taken up at the highest level. There is also a need for evolving a
mechanism for release of funds by project authorities in advance on yearly/half yearly basis. Only then, this problem is
likely to be solved, otherwise, this financial burden on KV Sangathan could continue to persist or may even increase.

KV Sangathan was in agreement with the recommendation of the Baldev Mahajan Committee that the Commissioner,
KVS should have full powers of opening of new sections and sanctioning additional staff. The Board of Governors had,
accordingly, decided to recommend the same to the Government. The Committee, however, finds that as per the latest
response received from the Department, the recommendations of the Baldev Mahajan Committee have since been rejected
in principle. The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for the change in the stand of the Government. The
Committee would like to point out that number of students in a class/section being more than the prescribed ratio, does
affect the quality of education adversely; it needs to be avoided. The Committee is also in favour of more and more
students getting admitted to the KVs. But overcrowding is certainly not conducive for focused attention on students’
performance. KVs cannot be an exception to this. The Committee, therefore, feels that all efforts need to be made to avoid
overcrowding in KVs by opening additional sections with all the infrastructure wherever needed.
 
Action Taken
Kendriya Vidyalayas primarily provide education to the wards of the transferable Central Govt. employees. These
employees get transferred to various metropolis and Kendriya Vidyalayas located in these cities/ state capitals have to
accommodate the children producing Transfer Certificate from another Kendriya Vidyalaya. One of the reasons of
overcrowding in KVs located in cities/state capitals is due to this factor. Use of special dispensation quota and demand
from Government employees for some centrally located KVs has put additional pressure. However, to ease the situation
new sections have been sanctioned in most of the KVs where infrastructure is available. To accommodate more students,
KVS has already started running of two shifts in 44 Kendriya Vidyalayas. In these KVs the problem of overcrowding has
eased to a certain extent. However, sections cannot be opened indiscriminately due to constraint of land and building
space. Within the capacity of the infrastructure, new sections are opened by KVS depending on need.
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee has been expressing its concern about certain problems faced in implementing the discretionary
quota for the Members of Parliament for admission in the Kendriya Vidyalayas.  One such problem relates to those
Members of the Lok Sabha who do not have Kendriya Vidyalaya in their constituencies.   As per the existing system, they,
of course, get the prescribed coupons but cannot recommend any admission under this quota.  It, thus, amounts to denying
this facility to such MPs.  The Committee, therefore, feels that this lacunae needs to be corrected immediately by allowing
MPs under this category either to recommend admission in a school situated in the neighbouring  constituencies or
anywhere in their State, as is the case with the Members of the Rajya Sabha.
VI.       VACANCY POSITION
Recommendations/Observations
6.1       In its 162
nd Report, the Committee had dealt with the problem of vacancies existing in different categories of
teaching staff in KVS.  The Committee found that the position remained very discouraging for a long time.   The
Committee notes that the selection of 1571 teachers in December 2003, in which certain procedural irregularities were
alleged to have been committed, continued to remain undecided till September 2006.  As a result, the appointment of the
teachers was withheld.   In the meantime, a Satyam Committee was appointed to look into the issues and the selected
teachers were given conditional appointment on ad hoc basis, till the Committee submitted its report.  Thus, the teachers
remained ad-hoc for more than three years.  In the meanwhile, the Committee learnt that the report of the Satyam
Committee has since been submitted to the Government.   The Committee notes with serious concern that the process of
selection of teachers that had started in February 2003, could not be completed till the time of the writing of this Report. 
The Committee is at a loss to see that 1571 posts of teachers continued to remain vacant for several years.  The
Committee, while appreciating the move for giving the ad hoc appointment to the selected teachers pending the inquiry,

197thReport of Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/197threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:42]
demands strict action against those found responsible for this fiasco.  The Committee calls upon the government to
consider the recommendations of the Satyam Committee for an early implementation so that future of those teachers is
decided without further delay.  The Committee is also aware that on an average about 7.5% adhoc teachers have
contractual appointment.  The Committee would like to point out that teachers appointed for a short period would have no
motivation to give good results, for obvious reasons.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that ad-hoc appointment
should be to the barest minimum and the vacancies must be filled as soon as possible.  The Committee also has serious
reservations about the prolonged recruitment procedure that goes on for years.  There is an urgent need for having a review
of the same for streamlining, decentralizing and eliminating the unnecessary procedural formalities.
 
Action Taken
Candidates, who had been selected for the post of PGT/TGT/PRT during 2003, were given provisional offer of
appointment on contract basis initially.   Later on these appointments were regularized in September, 2006 after
considering the findings of the Sathyam Committee.
KVS is in the process of another round of recruitment of teachers and the process is likely to be over by end of
September, 2007.
It is the policy of KVS to have the minimum possible number of  contractual teachers and that too mostly in cases
of unanticipated vacancies.
 
 
Recommendations/Observations
6.2       The Committee in its 162
nd Report had strongly advocated the need for having a decentralized – zone wise
recruitment for KV teachers, instead of the existing centralized procedure. The most obvious reason for having a
decentralization system is to avoid the inherent problems faced in a centralized recruitment system by the KVS and the
candidates coming from different part of such a vast country.  The Committee is of the firm view that centralized
recruitment system is of the main reasons for continuance of vacancies for long time affecting the academic environment
of the Vidyalayas.  The Committee therefore, reiterates its recommendations of decentralization of the recruitment process
for selection of candidates at zonal level so that it becomes convenient to people of different regions to participate in the
process which otherwise may not be possible for them.   It would also ensure proper representation of the candidates from
different parts of the country, particularly from NE States and J&K.
 
Action Taken
Prior to 1999 the direct recruitments to the teaching posts used to be made by short-listing the candidates on the
basis of pre-determined evaluation criteria taking into consideration the academic and professional achievements and co-
curricular activities followed by interviews.  Direct recruitment for the post of PRT, TGT and Misc. categories of teachers
was done at the regional level by constituting Selection Board.  Promotions to the aforesaid posts from feeder grades/ posts
used to be done centrally at the Hqrs.  The appointment of selected candidates was also done within the region.  The
promotions as well as appointment by direct recruitment of PGTs, Vice-principals and Principals were made centrally at
the HQ. level.  In this system while the candidates from the universities that give liberal marks used to get included in the
short-lists, while the relatively better candidates from the universities who do not give liberal marks could not make to the
lists.  In order to remove such disparities, it was decided on the recommendations of the Selja Committee to hold the
written examination to assess the real potential and capabilities of the candidates irrespective of the university or
institution from which they were coming.  Need was felt for centralization in the recruitment process in order to ensure
greater degree of objectivity, transparency, uniformity in standards and selection of teachers on the basis of proven merit
as independently assessed on a uniform and standard criteria. It was, therefore, decided to centralize the recruitment of all
teaching and non-teaching posts except Group ‘D’.   In the new system, all candidates who possess the requisite
qualifications prescribed for the post are required to take written examination and based on merit list, drawn on the basis of
their performance in written test & interviews, select panels are prepared.   The matter on decentralization of recruitments
was sent to Legal Adviser of KVS for his opinion.   He opined that the regional recruitment system if followed would lead
to innumerable litigations, as KVS cannot shut out outsiders from applying for any post.  It has been the experience of
KVS in the past that regional recruitment led to a lot of complications resulting in switching over to centralized
recruitment system. In KVS, posts are filled up on transfer also and if regional recruitment is resorted to and if posts are
filled up on transfer, disgruntled    persons approach the courts questioning the manner of filling up of posts.  Courts do
quash such filling up of posts by transfer.       So far as the representations of the candidates from different parts of the
country particularly from NE states and J&K are concerned, it is submitted that the advertisement for recruitment of
teachers is published in the Employment News (Weekly), National News papers and also in the local/vernacular News
Papers. Besides this each and every information relating to recruitment is uploaded on the website of KVS.  The

197thReport of Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/197threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:42]
publication and displaying on notice boards of the Regional Offices as well as in the Schools is also taken at length for
wide publicity in each and every corner of the country.  As such all-eligible candidates from any part of the country can
apply in response to Sangathan’s advertisement.  In fact teachers working in the Kendriya Vidyalayas belong to all parts of
the country.
 
Comments of the Committee
(Para 6.1 & 6.2)
The Committee does not agree with the arguments given by the Department against decentralization of recruitment
by Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan; it appears to be purely technical without appreciating the Committee’s concern.  The
Committee therefore, reiterates its recommendations for making decentralized recruitment in Kendriya Vidyalayas.  Steps
must be taken for removing the legal hurdles by framing suitable laws and regulations.
 
VII.      GRIEVANCES REDRESSAL
Recommendations/Observations
7.1       The Committee observes that some initiative has been taken by the KV Sangathan for strengthening the Grievance
Redressal Machinery.  Senior officers are visiting Regional Offices to attend to the grievances of employees.   Every day,
specific hours have been fixed at the KV Sangathan’s Headquarters when aggrieved employees can meet the concerned
officers including the Commissioner without prior appointment.  While appreciating the initiative taken by KV Sangathan,
the  Committee would like to point out that there should also be a mechanism whereby a track of efficacy of such an outlet
available to employees can be constantly monitored. The Committee feels that the ground reality in this regard seem to be
somewhat different.  Even public representatives such as MPs sometimes, fail to contact the concerned officers because
most of the time they are not available.  Details regarding number of Grievances received and those dealt with also do not
indicate a significant improvement. The Committee has learnt that teachers union in KVS has been de-recognised.   The
Committee would like to have a brief note on the issue for its consideration.
 
Action Taken
KVS has already implemented a Grievance Redressal Mechanism as formulated by Govt. of India.Besides above
visitors are attended to daily from 4.00 p.m. to 5.00 p.m. by all senior officers of KVS, HQ and Regional Offices without
prior appointment for redressal of their grievances. The Hon’ble representatives of the public are also attended to as and
when they visit the office and during meetings they are extended due courtesy.The brief note on status of teachers union is
given in Annexure-VIII.
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is not convinced with the Grievances redressal mechanism working in KVS, since there are no
details about the complaints received/ pending / redressal made during the last years. Without any supporting data, the
Committee is not able to judge the efficacy of the mechanism. 
 
VIII.     SURVEY OF KVs
Recommendations/Observations
8.1       The Committee is of the firm view that this is the right time for making a comprehensive assessment of KVs spread
over different parts of the country. Reason behind making such a suggestion is that Kendriya Vidyalayas having evolved
into a reputed educational system since its inception in 1960s have seen many ups and downs. In spite of the best efforts
put forth by all concerned, quite a few constraints continue to persist at the ground level. Committee’s specific
recommendation for conducting a detailed survey was meant to take corrective measures based on its findings so that KV
Sangathan is better equipped in attaining its goals. Committees recommendations /observations on the various aspects of
functioning of KVS are also meant for this purpose only.
 
Action Taken
An evaluation of KVS was conducted by a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri J.C. Pant, former Secretary
to Government of India in 2002. Need for another evaluation will be assessed by the Ministry.  Recommendations of the
Working Group on Secondary and Vocational Education constituted by the Planning Commission for the Eleventh Plan
will also be kept in view.
 
Recommendations/Observations
8.2       The Committee is unhappy to note that the spirit of Committee’s suggestions have not been given the importance
that they deserved by the Department/KV Sangathan. The Committee is afraid that development of an Information Booklet

and periodical submission of duly    filled–up Proforma by KVs would remain a routine exercise. The Committee would
again reiterate its recommendation for conducting a nation – wide survey of KVs and the information generated there from
for improving the functioning of KV Sangathan.
 
Action Taken
The Ministry and KVS attach the highest importance to the Committee’s recommendations and have been
benefited from many of their suggestions. The suggestion for the survey will be given due consideration.
 
Comments of the Committee
(para 8.1 & 8.2)
The Committee has been informed that an evaluation of KVs was conducted by a Committee under the
Chairmanship of Shri J.C. Pant, former Secretary to Government of India in 2002.  The Committee is not aware about the
mandate and area of evaluation of the Pant Committee.   A copy of the report of this Committee has also not been made
available to the Committee.  Against this backdrop, the stand taken by the Department that need for another evaluation of
KVs will be assessed by them is not acceptable to the Committee.   The Committee would also like to point out that
evaluation and survey are two different aspects.  The Committee therefore recommends that detailed survey of KVs as per
Committee's recommendation should be undertaken and completed at the earliest.

Comments of the Committee

not yielded any desired results.  The Committee observes that in most of the cases although land had been finally
earmarked by the sponsors, approval of the Ministry of  Defence / concerned State Government was awaited. The
Committee had called for a status report on this within three months.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that

The Committee takes a serious view of this.  The Committee is of the firm view that it is high time that the matter is taken
up at the highest level, be it the Ministry of Defence or any State Government.
The Committee observes that land is to be provided in respect of total 126 KVs.  38 KVs pointed out by the
Committee were the longest pending ones.  The Committee is of the view that with the relaxation in  land norms for
different areas, sponsoring agencies for KVs should be in a better position to provide the land.  The Committee,
accordingly, recommends that sponsoring agencies for all such KVs should be pursued vigorously for release of land in a
time-bound manner.

1.8       The Committee is also of the considered opinion that the tender documents must provide for heavy penalty on the
contractors if they fail to stick to the stipulated time frame fixed for this purpose.
Action Taken
The existing penalty clause has now been modified by the CPWD. As per new clause important milestones for
completion of the projects are to be defined in the tender documents. There is a provision of deduction of 1.5% per month
of delay of tender cost as a penalty in case of non-achievement of each milestone. (Copy enclosed at Annexure-V). The
new clause also provides submission of performance guarantee equivalent to 5% value of the work before signing the

II.        INFRASTRUCTURE
Recommendations/Observations
2.2       The Committee was informed that out of total 498 functional / established Navodaya Vidyalayas, 378 are
functioning at permanent sites in permanent buildings while 120 are functioning in temporary site in temporary  
buildings.   To add to the woes, 36 JNVs out of 378 permanent Vidyalayas do not have a playfield. To this 36 JNVs
another 120 temporary JNVs may be added. Thus a total of 156 JNVs are not having playfield out of the total 498
functional / established Vidyalayas. The Committee finds this situation very disturbing. The Committee is of considered
opinion that the sports help in improving physical & psychological strength of the children and further contribute in
development of overall personality of the children. It is a means of recreation as well. Absence of playfields, therefore, put
them at disadvantage in these regards. The Committee strongly emphasizes the need for making playfield mandatory and
where it is not possible due to small area available, alternate arrangements be made with neighbouring bodies, agencies,
clubs, etc. for allowing students to make use of their facilities.
Action Taken
As on date, 539 Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya (JNVs) are functional, out of which, 400 JNVs are functioning at
permanent site. 365 JNVs functioning at permanent site have been provided with proper playfields including 400 meter
track, football / hockey fields, basketball and volleyball courts. Similar playfields are under construction in remaining 35
JNVs functioning at permanent site. Facilities for volleyball, Kho-Kho and Badminton courts etc. are available at 139
JNVs functioning at temporary site also. Construction of Phase-A, which includes construction of playgrounds, for 109
JNVs functioning at temporary sites, is in progress. Efforts are on to provide playgrounds to all schools.
            Games and sports are made compulsory for all students in Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas. Invariably they start
morning with PT & morning physical exercises / yoga and in the evening for about an hour they are taken to games and
sports.

IV.       CRITERIA FOR ADMISSION IN NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
Recommendations/Observations
4.1       The Committee notes that the admission to Navodaya Vidyalayas is done on the basis of a Selection Test for
which, certain eligibility conditions have been laid down. The conditions inter alia provide that a candidate appearing for
the Selection Test must be studying in Class-V in a recognized school in that district where he / she is seeking admission.
Admission in Class-VI is given subject to the condition of passing Class-V before admission and also the candidate must
have studied and passed Class III, IV and V from recognized school / schools in the preceding three continuous academic
sessions for which the Selection Test is conducted, spending one full academic session in each class through the formal
system of education, without any repetition of class, gap and / or break in attendance.
Recommendations/Observations
4.2       The Committee notes that unscrupulous people are taking undue advantage of district criterion laid down in the
guidelines. The Committee finds that children of other districts take admission in absentia in Class V in educationally
backward districts where a JNV is situated while continuing their education in reputed schools in urban or semi-urban
areas. At the time of Selection Test, they compete against students of that district who are comparatively weaker, and thus
they have better chance to get admission meant for the rural students of that district. This peculiar aspect has remained
unnoticed and goes against the very basic idea of providing quality education to the rural students of a particular district.
The Committee is of the considered view that the condition of studying and passing Class-III, IV and V in preceding three
continuous sessions needs to be reviewed. The student aspiring for admission in a particular JNV should be asked to
produce a certificate of domicile of that particular district. This would be the most reasonable way to check the influx of
otherwise ineligible candidates.
Recommendations/Observations
4.3       The Committee wants to draw the attention of the Department towards the fact that a large number of poor farmers
and labourers are sending their children to so called `English schools’ running in their villages which are actually local,
private, small-time, non-recognized schools. Also, a good number of children are availing education in informal centres of
learning like EGS & AIE and others being run by the NGOs and supported by the Government. The Committee is not
aware whether children coming out from these non-recognized / informal centres  are eligible to get admission in their
district’s JNV. The Committee desires the Department to reconsider the concept of formal education and see that its aim to
provide quality education to meritorious poor rural students does not get defeated in the cobweb of guidelines which seems
to be a little  away  from  the  ground  reality prevailing in rural areas. The Committee strongly feels that a candidate
coming out of these informal centres or un-recognized school of the village be allowed to take the selection test once he or
she has passed Class-V.
Recommendations/Observations

VII.     PROBLEM OF DROP-OUT
Recommendations/Observations
7.1       The Committee notes that dropout is occurring in different classes of JNVs due to various reasons.  The Committee
finds the vacancies arising due to the drop-out are not being filled up before Class IX   for   the reason that the special
identity of JNVs would not be amenable to newly admitted students as they would not be able to adapt to the new
environment.  The Department has been informed that lateral entry is allowed only in Class IX, which is a stage when the
children are grown up, and special orientation programmes are conducted to bring them at par with regular students.  The
Committee does not agree to this notion of adaptability of students before Class IX.  It feels that the identity of the JNVs
should be made special in the sense that any child who joins the Vidyalaya at any stage must feel at home rather than
experiencing problem of adaptability.  Adaptability for a newcomer is a natural problem.  But the Samiti needs to devise
such teaching methods where the newcomer gets mentally and psychological settled and feels at home at the earliest.
Recommendations/Observations
7.2       Another problem against lateral entry before Class IX as explained by the Department before the Committee was
that holding an entrance test for every class every year is not a viable proposition.  The Committee is of the opinion that
the lateral entry must be allowed to fill up vacancies, if any, in all the classes and not merely in IX and XI classes to ensure
that no seat was allowed to go vacant.  It is a waste of the available resources.  The Committee is not inclined to agree with
the argument of the Department that the number of vacancies being small, it would not be viable to hold an entrance
system for every class every year.  The practice of entrance test is in vogue  in  all  schemes  of  school including private /
public school.  If entrance test could be held every year for VI, IX and XI classes other classes also can be clubbed with
them.  Furthermore, the Committee wishes to reiterate its recommendation about admitting girl students of the area in the
vacant seats.  The Committee desires that no seat be allowed to go vacant when lot of our children remains out of school.

II.        INFRASTRUCTURE
Recommendations/Observations
2.3       The Committee notes that the state of infrastructure in Navodaya Vidyalaya leaves lot to be desired. In its visit to
some JNVs, the Committee noticed that many Navodaya buildings were in bad shape with leaking ceilings, damp rooms,
plaster peeling off, unclean water tanks and the likes. The Committee regrets to note poor quality of construction upkeep
and maintenance of Navodaya Vidyalaya buildings, lack of proper cleanliness in toilets, hygiene in kitchen including the
hostels.
Recommendations/Observations
2.4       The Department conceded the poor maintenance of school buildings, despite the fact that certain amount is made
available to the every Vidyalaya for this purpose every year. The Department, however, argued that this amount was not
sufficient particularly in those cases where the requirement was high and in that situation a case is made out for special
maintenance grant, and to the extent possible, it is made available.
Action Taken
2.3 &2.4          CBRI, Roorkee, was appointed as the nodal agency for preparation of building designs and specifications at
the starting of the Navodaya Scheme during 1985. In order to economize the construction cost, double tier system in the

-           Principals  are encouraged to take up day to day maintenance at the Vidyalaya level by delegating more financial

V.        HOSTEL FACILITY
Recommendations/Observations
5.1       Navodaya Vidyalayas being residential schools need to have proper hostel facilities for their students. 
Committee’s attention has been particularly drawn by acute shortage of required staff for efficient running of Navodaya
Vidyalaya hostels.  Committee had accordingly made detailed observations and recommendations in this regard.  The
Committee is, however, disappointed by the follow-up action indicated by the Department.  One striking feature noticed
by the Committee was the acute shortage of Matrons for the Hostels.  One cannot deny the fact that Navodaya Vidyalayas
whether operating from temporary site or permanent site continue to be residential schools and need to have the required
manpower.  Committee’s pointed observation about there being only 36 posts of Matrons filled up against 339 sanctioned
posts has evoked the response that the directions have been noted for compliance. The Committee fails to understand
whether action if any is contemplated by the NVS / Department.  The Committee would like to reiterate that entrusting the
job of supervision of hostels to teachers can be considered only a stopgap arrangement.  Matrons specifically entrusted
with the supervision of hostel facilities to the enrolled students need to be there.  One must not forget that students enrolled
in Navodaya Vidyalayas include both girls and boys coming from different backgrounds and being in formative year of
their lives need to be handled in a professional and efficient manner, which requires 24 hour supervision.  The Committee
had also drawn the attention of the Department towards big gap between the sanctioned and in position status of other
hostel functionaries like Catering Assistant, cook, and storekeeper.  The Committee has been given to understand that
instructions have been issued to all Regional Offices to fill up vacant posts of non-teaching staff.  The Committee strongly
feels that a review of status of manpower available for the hostels of Navodaya Vidyalayas is required to be made on an
urgent basis and make the hostels functional in the real sense by providing the required staff.
Action Taken
It has been decided to provide one post of Matron for looking after girls students in all those Jawahar Navodaya
Vidyalayas where the strength of the girls students exceeds 100. Procedure for appointment of Matron has been simplified
and henceforth the appointment will be made at the school level. To reduce the delay in selection process, the Principal has
already been authorized to renew the contract of the Matron in case her services and performance are found satisfactory.
As on date, out of 366 sanctioned posts of Matron 208 have been filled. Specific directions have also been issued to all the
Regional Offices and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas to fill up the vacant posts of non-teaching staff by the end of June
2007.
            The status of manpower available for hostels will be reviewed by NVS.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee is happy to note that out of 366 sanctioned posts of Matron, 208 have been filled.  This can be
considered as a good achievement, keeping in view earlier 36 filled up posts of Matron.   The Committee would, however,
like to point out that there still remains a significant gap between the sanctioned (366) and filled up (208) posts of Matron. 
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that all out efforts should be made to get all the sanctioned posts filled up

5.2       The Committee had also emphasized the need for ensuring safety and security of students of Navodaya Vidyalayas.
However, the feedback received from the Ministry clearly indicates that all the Navodaya Vidyalayas cannot be considered
secure.  Navodaya Vidyalayas not having compound walls are yet to be identified.  Same is the position with regard to
light arrangements. The Committee takes a serious view of lack of security for the Vidyalayas.  Committee is of the firm
view that security aspect needs to be given priority especially in view of location of Navodaya Vidyalayas.  Boundary
walls and lighting arrangements being the minimum requirements needs to be provided to each and every Navodaya
Vidyalayas.  It would be appropriate if initiative is taken by the NVS for strengthening the same.  The Committee would
like to have a status note in this regard.
Action Taken
Compound wall / fencing have been provided in all JNVs except three JNVs at Surat, Chandrapur and Garhchiroli.
In these three JNVs compound wall could not be constructed due to land dispute (Annexure-XII & XIII).
            As per present policy for safety and security of students, compound wall of 2 mtr height (1.2 mtr masonry wall and
0.8 mtr barbed wire fencing) is being provided in all JNVs. However, in past i.e. till 1999 due to paucity of the funds, half
of the campus was provided with brick wall and remaining half with barbed wire fencing. The barbed wire fencing now is
in worn-out conditions at various locations. Samiti has taken steps to replace worn out barbed wire fencing with masonry
walls in a phased manner. Details status of boundary walls is placed at Annexure-XIV. On an average two security staff is
also posted in each vidyalaya.
            In all JNVs functioning at permanent site, electrical connections from the nearby rural / urban feeder have been
provided. However, majority of JNVs are connected with rural feeder wherever 10 to 12 hours load shedding is very
common. Samiti has been making efforts to connect all the Vidyalayas from the urban feeder to improve the lighting
arrangements in the JNVs.
            In all JNVs, 15 to 25 KVA DG Sets have been provided to supply electricity in case of load shedding.
            Samiti has been providing 40 to 50 streetlights in JNV complexes. All the JNVs, except 10, shifted in permanent
buildings have been provided with the streetlights. The streetlight works in remaining 10 JNVs is under progress. Detailed
status is placed at Annexure-XV.
            With a view to ensure safety and security of students, the Samiti has also issued detailed instructions and
guidelines, which have been widely circulated. In addition, the Samiti has prepared the following action plan to sensitize
the students and the staff with regard to safety and security aspects in the Vidyalaya.
i)
        All ROs will prepare detailed case studies of all death cases that have taken place in the region during last three years
giving detailed facts, factors responsible for such incident, negligence, if any on the part of administration,
contributory negligence on the part of student / parents and other relevant factors. These cases studies will be
compiled and circulated to all Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas and NLIs for further discussions and creating awareness
at all levels.
ii)
       Each RO will prepare a short video film highlighting the school specific safety hazards and potential threats to safety
of the children and the steps that may be taken to prevent accidents.
iii)     Entire staff including non-teaching staff should be taken into confidence with regard to school specific safety issues

iv)     House system should be strengthened to use it for understanding and significant behaviour changes or deviations,
conduct, health and adolescent related problems of the students. The Principals should regularly interact with
housemasters and house captains in this regard.
v)      Value education in Navodaya Vidyalayas should be institutionalized.
All existing instructions with regard to safety and security of students issued by the Samiti should be consolidated.
These should also be reviewed to identify the areas, which require maximum monitoring for safety and security of
children, and should be reiterated.
Comments of the Committee

            The Committee is not inclined to consider the existing medical facilities at JNVs as adequate.  The Committee

VI.       PENSIONARY BENEFITS TO NVS EMPLOYEES
Recommendations/Observations
The Committee reiterates its recommendation made in its 154
th Report for provision of pensionary benefits to the
NVS employees on the same level as being given to the KVS employees.  The Committee strongly feels that NVS
employees need to be governed by similar service conditions including pensionary benefits as applicable to KVS
employees.  The Committee fails to understand the rationale for adoption of a discriminatory approach by the Government
towards an autonomous body having, broadly speaking, the same mandate as the other.  The Committee is not convinced
by the contention of the Department that an organization having Contributory Provident Fund Scheme should continue to
be governed by that scheme as the new Pension Scheme was only applicable to the organizations which earlier had GPF-
cum-Pension Scheme prior to 1-1-02.  The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department towards similar
recommendation made by the Expert Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of Shri Y.N. Chaturvedi in June 2001
to review the Management structure and operating mechanism of NVS.  The Committee would like to emphasize that the
Department should approach the Ministry of Finance once again in this regard.
Action Taken
The introduction of pension scheme was earlier taken up in consultation with the Ministry of Finance, but could not
be agreed to due to resource crunch and the efforts of the Government to maintain the budgetary deficit within the desired
limit.  The matter is again under consideration of this Ministry.
Comments of the Committee
            Committee has been informed that the matter of provision of pensionary benefits to NVS employees is again under
the consideration of the Ministry.  The Committee would like the Department to expedite and positively introduce the
pensionary benefits for the NVS employees.

                   NORMS FOR OPENING OF NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is happy to note some progress in the sanctioning of new JNVs and making them functional
during the last year.  As on 31
st January, 2007, out of 565 JNVs sanctioned, 539 JNVs have been made functional.  Out of
26 non-functional JNVs, 14 JNVs have been sanctioned during 2006-07.  The Committee would, however, like to point
out that out of 21 non-functional JNVs  existing at the time of presentation of the 184 th Report in November 2006, only 9
JNVs could be made functional till 31st January 2007.  The Committee would like to know the reasons for such delay.   It
recommends the Department and the NVS to take urgent measures to make all the JNVs sanctioned before 2006-07,
functional during 2007 itself.  It also desires that 14 JNVs sanctioned during 2006-07 must also be made functional in the
next academic year.                                                      (Para 1.1)
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee would reiterate that the Department while ensuring to establish one school in each district of the
country, must insist on suitable temporary accommodation before sanctioning the schools.  Otherwise, as has been the
experience, the process of making schools functional gets delayed for a long time.
   (Para 1.3)
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee notes that out of 84 JNVs sanctioned in the NER, 8 JNVs continue to be non-functional, mainly
due to non-availability of temporary accommodation.  The Committee observes that there is no likelihood of situation
improving in the near future.  The Committee is also not aware about the constraints being faced by the concerned State
Governments in making the required land available.  But the fact remains that there is an urgent and greater need for
setting up JNVs in this remote and backward area of the country.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the
Department should pursue this matter with the concerned authorities at the highest level.
            The Committee notes that in respect of JNVs at Aizwal, Chimtuipui (Lawngtlai) and Lunglei, lands have been
transferred and the construction works sanctioned.  Construction activities are going to be started in the near future.  The
Committee feels that only constant monitoring at every level will ensure the completion of the projects at the earliest.  The
Committee would appreciate if the Department takes up this task on priority, and ensures no laxity at any level.
                                                                                                            (Para 1.4)
