4.4       REFINANCE CORPORATION/STUDENTS LOAN SCHEME
Recommendations/observations
4.4.1    The Committee is given to understand that the students who intend to avail educational loans from the banks are faced with
numerous procedural difficulties. The Department informed the Committee that banks were supposed to grant education loans to
students without insisting for any collateral security. Some cases of violation of this norm have however come to the notice. The
Department has also informed that the average loan given per student comes to a meager Rs.2 lakh. It has also come to the notice
of the Department that during the period when the student is undergoing a programme or a technical course, the banks start
demanding the interest liability. The Department is of the view that there should be a moratorium for at least one year after the
student completes his course. It is against this backdrop that the Department proposes to set up a Refinance Corporation to provide
some avenues to enable the students to mitigate their financial problems. The assistance will be in the form of loans with low rate
of interests. The Department has further informed that the matter is being taken up with the Planning Commission.
4.4.2    The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that the banks are violating the norms of disbursal and charging high
interest on educational loans to students.  The Committee in its 172
nd report had suggested to have a loan-disbursing agency
specifically for the students.  It is happy to note that the Department has proposed to set-up a Refinance Corporation for this
purpose.  The Committee recommends that the matter may be immediately taken up with the Planning Commission and
Department of Banking for working out/deciding necessary modalities for this purpose during this fiscal itself. The formation of
the Refinance Corporation to help the needy students who intend to pursue higher education cannot wait any further in the current
scenario.
Action Taken
            The concern expressed by the Committee regarding the high rates of interest on Student Loans was taken up at a meeting
with the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission, and a scheme of interest-subsidy is being worded out for which
adequate outlays are expected to be available during the 11
th Plan period.

development of micro enterprises and development of competency based curricula for effective skill transfer. The Committee
however did not find any mention of any recommendation to address the problem of uneven distribution of Community
Polytechnics in the country. Of the 669 Community Polytechnics in the country, the Eastern region has the least number i.e., 97 of
them compared to the North, West and South which have 187, 145 and 240 respectively. This position was even more disturbing
for the fact that the Eastern region was a backward region having the highest concentration of rural population. To a specific query
in this regard, the Department accepted the fact that all the Govt./Govt.-aided polytechnics of the North-Eastern region have not
been covered under the scheme. Out of a total number of 29 such polytechnics in the region, as many as 10 of them were yet to be
covered under the scheme. The Department has informed that these polytechnics could not be covered under the scheme since there
was no provision for expansion in the approved scheme during the 10
th Plan period. The Committee recalls that the Department on
the insistence of the Committee had taken up the matter of augmenting the strength of Community Polytechnics in the North-
Eastern region with the concerned State Governments. The Department in its action taken report to the Committee had then stated
that the State Governments had expressed their inability to open fresh Polytechnics but could consider opening more extension
counters of the existing polytechnics in that region. 
5.5.3    The Committee is of the considered opinion that the uneven reach of the Scheme in the Eastern region of the country does
not conform to its objective of securing community/rural development. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to factor
in this aspect while reviewing the Scheme for the 11th Plan.
Action Taken
            The Recommendation of the Committee has been noted and will be considered while reviewing and revamping the scheme
during the XIth Five Year Plan.

3.3       INDIAN INSTITUTE OF ADVANCED STUDY, SHIMLA
Recommendations/observations
3.3.1    Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla is a residential Institute of higher learning in all areas of Humanities, Social
Sciences, Indian Culture and Linguistics, providing congenial environment to eminent scholars and Fellows to concentrate on their
respective research projects.
3.3.2    The Committee has come across a number of irregularities in the functioning of the Institute.  The Department in a Special
Audit Report has pointed out a very disturbing fact about the Bye-laws of the Institute. The terms and conditions of grant of

CHAPTER - III
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/202ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:44:46]
fellowships are determined by the 'Governing Body' according to the directives of the Government issued from time to time and in
the light of revision of emoluments of fellows in other research organization of the M/o Human Resource Development. Unlike the
Indian Council for Historical Research (ICHR) which contains a stipulation in its Research Funding Rules that a candidate who is
selected for fellowship would require to furnish an undertaking in a prescribed proforma to the effect that if he leaves the
fellowship prematurely in the midway without completing the research project/manuscripts, he would have to refund the entire
amount of fellowship paid to him till that date.   This condition binds the fellow to complete the research work/monographs.  In the
Rules and Regulations and Bye-laws of the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla, there is no such stipulation or condition.  
As a result, a good number of fellows did not submit their monographs and the Institute could neither insist upon them to submit
the same nor take any action against them and suffered a loss of Rs.13.83 lakh as fellowship grants paid to such fellows.
3.3.3    Another disturbing fact brought out in the Special Audit Report is that as many as 37 fellows had not submitted their
monographs or their monographs were not worth publication or the fellows got the monographs published on their own.  Thus the
monographs could not be published which ultimately defeated the very purpose of the Institute and thereby incurred a wasteful
expenditure to the tune of Rs.93.36 lakh on fellowship grants paid to fellows.
3.3.4    The other equally disturbing findings of the Report are related to the unauthorized expenditure of Rs.7.86 lakh on billing
charges of the mobile phones issued to non-entitled officers, irregular purchase of telephones, outstanding contingency advances
and blockage of funds to the extent of Rs.200 lakh due to slow progress of special repair and maintenance of R.P. Niwas.
3.3.5    The Committee views the findings of the Special Audit Report with serious concern.   It is a pointer to the gross
mismanagement prevalent in the Institute. The Committee recommends that the Rules similar to that of Research Funding Rules of
ICHR may be made applicable to the fellowships granted by the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla.   It also recommends
that the persons found responsible for financial irregularities and other malpractices be brought to book and action be initiated
against them.  The Committee, therefore, desires that the Department take up the matter with the Institute and submit a report to the
Committee within one month from the presentation of this Report.
Action Taken
(paras 3.3.1 to 3.3.5)
As desired by the Hon'ble Committee, the matter was taken up with the IIAS, Shimla which has reported that action has
already been taken regarding the financial irregularities on account of irregular provision of mobile phones and the same have been
withdrawn from non-entitled officials.  As far as fellowship programme is concerned the institute has stated that it has a system of
concurrent monitoring of the research being conducted by its Fellows.  There is now a six monthly review process in place to
monitor the progress made in their research by the fellows as evaluated by experts from the relevant field.  It may be submitted that
the scheme of Fellowships at the ICHR does not require residential presence of its Fellows nor is there any method of constant peer
group review and interaction.   According to the institution, the level of scholarship expected by the IIAS is far higher than that
expected in a Council pertaining to research in a specific field.
            While not denying that the Fellows should reasonably be expected to submit their monograph before the end of their tenure,
the Institute had differed with the view adopted in the Special Audit Report regarding non-submission of monographs as the sole
pointer to mismanagement of the Fellowship programme.  The Institute has assured that it would initiate a revision of the system of
monitoring of the Fellowship programme to instill accountability both at the level of the Fellows as well as the Institute
Administration so that such a situation does not arise again.   According to the IIAS it would be able to report the action taken after
the revised Fellowship programme is considered by the Institute's Governing Body in its 2
nd quarterly meeting of the 2006-07
scheduled for October 2007.  In view of this the Hon'ble Committee is requested to extend the time for submission of the Report
directed to be submitted by the Ministry.
Comments of the Committee
(paras 3.3.1 to 3.3.5)
The Committee is happy to note that the Institute has decided to revise the monitoring system for its Fellowship
programme. It also hopes that the revised programme must have by now been considered by the Institute's Governing Body which
was scheduled to meet in October, 2007. The Committee expects the Department to submit its Report in the matter at the earliest.
3.5       FAKE UNIVERSITIES
Recommendations/observations
3.5.1    According to the UGC Act, 1956, the right of conferring or granting degrees shall be exercised only by a University
established or incorporated by or under a Central Act, or a State Act, or an Institution deemed to be University or an institution
specially empowered by an Act of Parliament to confer or grant degrees. Similarly, no institution other than a University
established or incorporated by or under a Central Act, or a State Act shall be entitled to have the word ‘University’ associated with
its name in any matter whatsoever.
3.5.2    To a specific query regarding the fake Universities identified and the action taken against them, the Department in its reply
stated that the UGC has detected 19 fake Universities/Institutions which are operating in violation of Section 22 of the UGC Act,

CHAPTER - III
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/202ndreport.htm[01-07-2016 15:44:46]
1956. The Department has further informed that out of these 19 fake Universities/Institutions, the UGC is yet to initiate legal
proceedings in respect of 6 of them, namely Gandhi Hindi Vidyapith, Allahabad (U.P.); DDB Sanskrit University, Puttur(T.N.); St.
John’s University, Kishanattam (Kerala); Raja Arabic University, Nagpur; Keserwani Vidyapith, Jabalpur and ADR-Centric
Judicial University, New Delhi, for want of full relevant details about these institutions.
3.5.3    A perusal of the status of the legal proceedings initiated against the 13 fake Universities/Institutions reveals that in most of
the cases, proceedings are likely to continue for long. In some cases, UGC is awaiting replies from the State Governments whereas
in some other cases, response is awaited from the police authorities. In the other cases, sessions of stays-counter stays, affidavits-
counter affidavits are on between the UGC and the fake Universities/Institutions. 
3.5.4    The Committee is of the considered opinion that the delay in the settlement of the cases gives rise to a situation of utter
confusion wherein both the parties claim to be on the right side of the law.  As a result, fake Universities/Institutions are taking
advantage of this confusion and continue to cheat the public. The Committee, therefore, urges the Department to take expeditious
action against fake universities/institutions under the existing regulations and rules.  Necessary legal sanctions be put in place
including by approaching Parliament for this purpose.  The Committee also strongly feels that there is an urgent need for giving
wide publicity about the existence of such fake universities.  Merely putting the list of approved universities on the website of UGC
will not serve the purpose.  Both Department and UGC need to be more pro-active in this regard simply because future of our
young students is involved.
Action Taken (paras 3.5.1 to 3.5.4)
In view of the observations of the Hon'ble Committee, the matter since been taken up with the University Grants Commission
(UGC) again requesting them to be more proactive in getting the fake universities/institutions closed down as early as possible.  
Since such institutions operate in violation of the UGC Act, 1956, it is incumbent on the part of the UGC to tackle such illegal
activities and, if necessary, to lodge FIR with the police as soon as the existence of such institutions comes to its notice.   This
Ministry has again directed UGC on 9
th August, 2007 to take a more proactive role in getting the fake universities/institutions
closed down as early as possible as there was inordinate delay in initiating legal action in as many as 6 cases and the proceedings in
13 other cases were also found to be conducted in a lackadaisical manner.  The UGC has also been advised to strengthen its
Malpractices Cell and to make it more accountable.  The need for starting more vigorous campaign in the print media against fake
universities/institutions has also been emphasized.
            The UGC has informed that it has issued Public Notice/Press Release in June, 2007 through some leading Newspapers,
cautioning the aspiring students about the fake Universities identified by it.
            The Ministry of Human Resources Development is separately formulating a proposal for strengthening the existing legal
framework with a view to ensuring deterrent punishment to fake institutions that function in contravention of the UGC Act, 1956.
Comments of the Committee
(paras 3.5.1 to 3.5.4)
The Committee notes that the Department has put the blame squarely upon the UGC for not being able to deal with the
problem in an efficient and effective manner. It, however, feels that the UGC is perhaps unable to take appropriate action in this
regard due to lack of adequate and stringent legal measures which the Department has indicated to be working on.  The Committee,
therefore, calls upon the Department to expedite the process for strengthening of the existing legal framework to pin down such
fake universities.  The Committee would also appreciate if a status note on the progress made in the legal proceedings initiated/to
be initiated against the 19 fake universities identified by UGC, is submitted to it at the earliest.  The Committee would like to point
out that there is an urgent need for making student/parents aware about existence of such fake universities.   A mechanism can
easily be evolved by seeking the co-operation of State Education Departments.

provide detailed information regarding the total number of distance education institutions that are functioning in the Central, State
and private domains.

the existence of unapproved distance education institutions would not serve the purpose.  Need of the hour is pro-active approach

nd Report on 'University and Higher Education',
stressed on the need for giving the DEC an independent statutory status like the UGC. Till date, the Department has been assuring

V      RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL CRECHE SCHEME FOR THE CHILDREN
        OF WORKING MOTHERS    
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 5.4           The Committee was informed that all these three organizations have experience of implementing crèche
programme across the country for almost three decades and have a nation-wide presence and network for running crèches. 
These organizations are well equipped with field units and staff.  Hence no constraints are being faced for implementation of
the scheme through these organizations. The Committee recommends that to meet the growth in number of creches other
organization/NGOs may also be involved in the implementation of these projects.
 
Action Taken
 
To meet the growing need of creches, the Ministry has prepared an EFC paper to open more creches across the country
during the 11th Five Year Plan. While expanding the scheme, due consideration will be given to the recommendations made by
the Committee by involving other reputed organizations/NGOs also for implementation of the crèche programme.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 5.8           The Committee notes that there are a large number of working mothers in unorganized sector who are in great
need of creches to look after their children when they go to work.  The safety of the children is utterly neglected and they are
prone to score of anti social elements.  Unfortunately, the crèche scheme is not functioning in those areas which need the
most.  The Committee was informed that for opening creches, applications are pending but the Ministry has no funds available
to open the creches.  The Committee therefore recommends that more allocation should be made under this head to meet the
growing demand for creches.  The Scheme may be revamped and expanded and the Planning Commission should be
approached for more allocation emphasizing the need for creches in view of safety of children of working mothers.
 
Action Taken
 
Efforts are being made to revamp and expand the scheme so as to ensure the safety of  the children of the working
mothers. An EFC Memo has been moved for this purpose.

HOMES FOR INFANT AND YOUNG CHILDREN FOR PROMOTION OF IN-COUNTRY ADOPTION

.X.       CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AGENCY (CARA)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 11.3         Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls is another new scheme proposed to be launched
after merger of two schemes, Kishori Shakti Yojana and Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls. The Committee observes
that NPAG was implemented on a pilot basis in 2002-03 and 2003-04 by the Planning Commission It continued on a pilot
project basis in 51 identified backward districts in 2006-07 also. Kishori Shakti Yojana has been there under ICDS for a few
years. It was only in 2006-07 that the scheme has been expanded from 2000 ICDS projects to 6118 ICDS projects. Committee
is not aware whether there is going to be a significant modification by bringing these two schemes under a new scheme.  The
Committee would, however, like to emphasise that there is a need for having a comprehensive review of all the Schemes
relating to nutrition for women and children being run not only by the Ministry of Women and Child Development but by
other Ministries like Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Rural Development etc.  The Committee strongly feels that there
should be an umbrella scheme for provision of nutrition to women and children under which different small schemes run by
other Ministries can be brought together.
 
Action Taken
 
 Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls  is proposed to be launched on merger of Kishori Shakti
Yojana and Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls. A proposal for expansion of NPAG to all districts and its merger with
KSY has been included in the XI Plan proposals of the Ministry.  This is necessary to improve the nutritional status of
adolescent girls and also to empower them socially and economically.
 
 The current efforts for addressing the issues of adolescent girls need to be stepped up substantially in an integrated manner. It
is necessary to expand  NPAG [which at present is being implemented in 51 identified districts only] and merge it with   KSY, 
enrich content and expand coverage of merged scheme to all the districts in the country in the XI Plan.  An integrated approach
taking care of life skills, nutrition, health of adolescents may pave way for a healthy society/ better quality human resources. It
would also lead to reduction in IMR/ MMR.
 
The two schemes are planned to be merged since they exist with more or less similar interventions, for the same group of
target beneficiaries. There are no significant modifications as such, envisaged in the new scheme.            However, the
provision for KSY which was prescribed, in the year 1991, as Rs.1.1 lakh per block per annum, is proposed to be revised upto
Rs.5 lakh per block per annum.  This will enrich the content, strengthen the training component and improve the quality of
services by making the interventions more meaningful.
 
 The  ICDS Scheme is not exclusively a Nutrition Scheme, but aims at holistic development of children below 6 years of age
and pregnant women and lactating mothers, through a package of 6 services viz. supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring,
nutrition and health education, immunization,  referral and pre-school education.  Three of the services i.e.  immunization,
referral services and health check up are provided in convergence with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

III.
             INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES SCHEME (ICDS)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
 Para 3.4          Besides that, States like Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat and West Bengal have exceeded the allocated funds, thereby
indicating that funds from the previous year were also available with them.  Both the situations indicate that some inherent
problem-areas continue to persist under the Scheme.  Either the Central funds are not reaching the implementing agencies in
time or States simply do not have the capacity to utilize the enhanced allocation.  The Committee understands that there
already exists a comprehensive four-level monitoring mechanism for ICDS.  The Committee can only emphasise that there is a
need for strengthening the monitoring mechanism so as to regulate the flow of funds and judicious utilization thereof
 
Action Taken
 
The funds released under ICDS Scheme are for committed liabilities towards salaries of ICDS functionaries,  honoraria
of Anganwadi Workers & Helpers and rents etc. Till the year 2006-07 funds were  released to States/UTs generally in two
instalments.  However, in some cases, additional instalments were released in the later part of the year due to reasons like late
receipt of Statements of Expenditure etc. As a result some unspent balances were there with the States/UTs as on 31.12.2006.
 
In pursuance to the directions of Ministry of Finance, from the current financial year i.e. 2007-08, the release of funds
to the States/UTs would be made in four instalments.  To monitor the expenditure more effectively, the release of instalments
has further been linked to receipt of Statement of Expenditure/Monthly Progress Report of the preceding quarter.  This would
lead to reduction in unspent balances at the end of each quarter.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 3.13  The Committee is aware that the ICDS was envisioned as a community participative programme and the
components of the scheme do not provide for the creation of infrastructural facilities.  However, in view of the present dismal
status of AWC buildings and also chronic problem of fund constraints being faced by majority of States, it is now time that
providing infrastructural facilities like construction of pucca building and other related aspects form part of the scheme so that
over a period of time all the AWCs must have pucca building to function.  If the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan can provide 30% of
its allocation for infrastructure development, the Committee does not find any reason why a particular percentage of the fund
could not be allocated for infrastructure creation under the ICDS.
 
Action Taken 
 
Taking cognizance of the fact that there is no provision for construction of AWCs under the  ICDS Scheme, except in

the World Bank Assisted Projects and in NE States as special dispensation, as also the findings of Rapid Facility Survey
conducted by NCAER, the lack of infrastructure has been identified as a cause for concern by the Ministry also.
 
To address this issue, the Government under the proposed revamped ICDS Scheme is contemplating infrastructural
development, on the pattern of SSA/NRHM. It is proposed to earmark 30% of the funds allocated for the ICDS scheme for
infrastructure development, including construction of AWC buildings, baby friendly toilets, provision of safe drinking water
etc.  
Since the number of AWCs without adequate infrastructure is very large, it has also been decided to explore the
possibilities of tapping the funds available under existing Schemes/Programmes of other Ministries also such as the National
Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), Backward Region Grant Fund (BRGF), MPLAD, Scheduled Caste Sub Plan
(SCSP), Tribal Area Sub Plan (TASP), etc.  These Ministries have already been requested to consider modifying their existing
guidelines to earmark certain percentage of allocation for construction of Anganwadi Centres.
 
Simultaneously, provision of safe drinking water and toilet facility in an Anganwadi Centre is also being attempted
through convergence with Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme, Total Sanitation Campaign being administered by the
Department of Drinking Water Supply under the Ministry of Rural Development.

Action Taken
 
            As per Section 4 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, the State Government, by

running the existing homes in the UT . They are meeting the expenditure from their  State Budget.

As per Section 8(1) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, any State Government may
establish and maintain either by itself or under an agreement with voluntary organisations, observation homes in every district
or a group of districts, as may be required for the temporary reception of  any juvenile in conflict with law during the pendency
of any inquiry regarding them under this Act.
 
As per Section 34(1) of the Act, the State Government may establish and maintain either by itself or in association with
the voluntary organisations, children’s home, in every district or group of districts, as the case may be, for the reception of
child in need of care and protection during the pendency of any inquiry and subsequently for their care, treatment, education,
training, development and rehabilitation.
           
There is no restriction on the number of homes to be set up by the State Government for the juveniles under the Act. It
is subject to conditions that (i) homes has been set up/notified by the State Governments in the Official Gazette; and (ii) the
State Government has made necessary budget provision in the State Budget to meet 50 per cent expenditure of these homes.

From the above, it is seen that though the unspent balance under ICDS increased from Rs 61 crore on 31.03.06 to Rs
156.91 crore by the end of December 2006, by the end of March 2007 there is a negative balance. It may be noted here that in
the major schemes like ICDS where large release of funds is involved some amount of unspent balance is inevitable. For
instance the total release under ICDS in 2006-07 was to the tune of Rs. 2691.38 crore.  However, it is invariably ensured by
the Ministry that unspent balances available with States and implementing agencies are always taken into account before
further releases are made.
 
Under Swayamsidha also, the funds are released to State Governments on continuous basis only after they have
reported at least 80% expenditure of the grant released to them.   In order to ensure proper fund utilization, the expenditure
position of States is reviewed in each quarter with the State Nodal Officers for Swayamsidha. It is felt that that unspent balance
with States is the amount they require to run the programme.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is constrained to observe that there is only marginal improvement in the pendency of Utilization
Certificates as per the updated information submitted to it by the Ministry.  Against 6765 UCs reported last, total number of
pending UCs as on 31
st July, 2007 is 6467.  What is more worrisome is that against the maximum number of 4697 outstanding
UCs pertaining to the earliest period (1986-87 to 2001-02), latest figures are 4679.  The Committee is compelled to conclude
that serious efforts and constant review claimed to have been made by the Ministry have failed to make any impact on the UCs
outstanding for last two decades.  The Committee also apprehends that records for this period may not be available with the
Ministry.  Had they been available, Committee’s direction for furnishing details of implementing agencies (State-wise,
Scheme-wise) which were yet to submit UCs would not have remained unattended.  The Committee would appreciate if this
information is furnished by the Ministry without any further delay. 
 
Committee had made specific observation on the availability of unspent balance under two major schemes .i.e ICDS
and Swayamsiddha.  The Committee finds that under ICDS, position has improved considerably by showing negative balance
by the end of March, 2007.  The Committee would, however, like to point out that in the absence of details from four States -
Bihar, Goa, Kerala and Uttranchal, this improvement level cannot be considered totally correct.  The Committee is also not
inclined to agree with justification given by the increasing unspent balcnce from Rs. 13.70 crore as on 1
st  April, 2006 to Rs.
18.86 crore as on 1 st April 2007 under Swayam Siddha Scheme.  To say that unspent balance with States is the amount
required for running the scheme defeats the very basis of implementation of a scheme with targets fixed and funds allocated
for every quarter and reviewed by the Department with State Nodal officers.
 
The Committee has been given to understand that grants are released in respect of those organizations whose UCs are
pending only when relaxations are obtained from the Ministry of Finance on case-to-case basis, keeping in mind the smooth
functioning of the schemes.  The Committee finds it hard to believe that the Ministry of Finance would have given relaxation
in a routine manner keeping in view such a large number of UCs remaining outstanding for yeas together.
 
            The Committee reiterates the need for evolving an effective monitoring mechanism for the clearing of pending UCs. 
Also, the Committee recommends the Ministry to guide the States Govts/statutory bodies/NGOs in clearing the pending UCs
and also to adopt a concept of fiscal responsibility for better fiscal management.  Hence, the Committee urges the Ministry to
make concerted efforts for solving this pressing problem of pendency of UCs.

Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 3.10         The Committee strongly recommends that immediate corrective measures need to be initiated on the gap areas
highlighted in the NIPCCD Study.  If this is the state of affairs after more than thirty years of ICDS being launched and crores
of funds being provided under the Flagship Scheme of the Ministry, then it would be better if the so-called multi-level
monitoring mechanism is simply done away with.
 
Action Taken   
 
The Evaluation Study entitled ‘Three Decades of ICDS: An Appraisal’ conducted by NIPCCD in December, 2006 was
circulated to all State Governments/UTs.  A presentation was also made in the Conference of State Secretaries dealing with
ICDS requesting them to take urgent steps to rectify the deficiencies pointed in the Study.
 
It may, however, be noted that ever since its launch in 1975, the Scheme does not provide for construction of AWC
building or safe drinking water/sanitation facilities in the AWCs.  It was envisaged that the local community would provide the
infrastructure.  There has been, though, provision for hiring a suitable building on rent. To enable the Angawandi Workers to
deliver the services under the Scheme efficiently, it has been proposed to provide for construction of AWC building including
kitchen and toilet in the 11th Five Year Plan. Action has been intensified to provide safe drinking water and toilet facilities in
the anganwadi centre through convergence with schemes like Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme, Total Sanitation
Campaign being administered by the Ministry of Rural Development.  Efforts are also being made, as the requirement of funds
is very large, to explore the possibility of utilizing funds available under existing schemes of various Ministries like NREGA,
Backward Region Grant Fund, MPLADS and SCSP, TASP etc. for strengthening the infrastructure at AWC.
 
The Statements of Expenditure sent by the States have a column specifying procurement of PSE kits.  It is reflected
from the SOEs  that some of the States were not procuring PSE kits as per their entitlement. These States have been requested
to procure the same at the earliest so that the benefit of PSE reaches all the beneficiaries.  There is a provision of Rs. 5000/- in
the Scheme for purchase of cooking and serving utensils among other things at the time of operationalisation of AWCs.  There
is also a provision of contingencies at AWCs level of Rs. 600/- which could be used for replacement of utensils.
 
It has also been observed from the expenditure statement received as on  31.3.07 that many States have spent more than
their allocated share of Supplementary Nutrition. However, (12 out of 23 which reported) States which have not been incurring
90 per cent of their estimated expenditure of the SNP budget were requested to spend as per the norms by providing adequate
funds in their budget of 2007-08 (Assam and Orissa are part of theses 12).
 
The States have also been requested to utilize the available amount of Rs 25,000 per project for IEC activities so that

Comments of the Committee
 
Committee’s attention has been drawn by the disturbing findings brought out in an Evaluation Study entitled ‘Three
Decades of ICDS: An Appraisal’ conducted by NIPCCD in December, 2006.  In response to Committee’s recommendation for
initiating corrective measures, the Ministry has come forward with a detailed reply,  outlining the various initiatives to be
taken to provide the required infrastructure and basic facilities at AWCs.  The Committee is dismayed to note that it has taken
more than three decades for the Ministry to realize that AWCs were lacking the minimum facilities and participation of local
community was simply not there.  The Committee can only say that the task ahead is very difficult as convergence of various
schemes handled by different Ministries is proposed during the 11
th  plan for making AWCs functional in the real sense. 
Relying only on the Statements of Expenditure sent by the State Governments for analyzing the judicious utilization of
allocated funds will not serve the purpose now. 
            The Committee would like to emphasize that in the backdrop of States failing to effectively implement the Scheme,
due to one reason or the other, Centre need to play a more pro-active role.  This can be easily done by making surprise visits,
analyzing with State implementing agencies the problem areas and finding out the ways and means to tackle the same.  The
Committee strongly feels that along with the implementing agencies, time has also come for reaching out to the targeted
beneficiaries directly. Once, they are made aware, through media and local authorities, the multi-level monitoring mechanism
will get the real strength and lead to fulfillment of all the objectives of this Flagship Scheme of the Ministry.

Para 3.14         The Committee notes that Ministry is doing all out efforts to universalize the ICDS Scheme.  The Secretary
submitted before the Committee that there seems to be a lack of motivation at the grass-root level and there is a case for a
much stronger community participation.             The Committee feels that the Ministry should come forward to revamp,
redesign and recast the ICDS scheme in all possible ways.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 3.16   The Committee recommends that since the flow of money from the Centre to the Implementing agencies is taking
lot of time, efforts may be made for quicker and expeditious dispersal of money.  If need be, the ICDS scheme may be
converted into a Mission Mode Scheme so that intermediate agencies can be removed.
 
Action Taken   (Paras 3.14 & 3.16)
 
            To mould the ICDS Scheme to suit the present day requirements, a proposal to revamp the Scheme and  implement it in
a “Mission Mode” in the 11
th Plan on the pattern of Sarv Siksha Abhiyan (SSA)/ National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), is
under active consideration.  
          
Under the restructured ICDSScheme, delegation of financial and administrative powers is also contemplated. To allow
for greater flexibility in flow of funds, it is proposed to set up  State and District level Societies which would be registered and
would prepare a District Child Development Plan and the Central funds would flow to the District Society through the State
Society as in the case of NRHM and SSA.
           
The concept of flexi funds is also proposed to be introduced with a view to enable the Committees at District Block and
Village levels to utilize funds as per locally identified needs and  priorities.
          
To tackle the problem of lack of motivation at the grass roots level, involvement of the community through PRIs, Self-
Help Groups of Women, Stake-holders Committee such as the Mothers Committee, etc. is envisaged in the 11
th Plan so that
ICDS becomes a truly community-driven rather than government-driven programme.   
 
 In the XI Plan, public-private partnership is also proposed to be encouraged to leverage the strength of the private (not
for profit) sector entities in implementation, supervision and monitoring of the Scheme.

Family Welfare so far in administering SSA and NRHM in Mission Mode may be shared by the Ministry so as to ensure a
fully effective monitoring mechanism under ICDS. 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 3.18         From 2005-2006, the Government of India were to support states upto 50% of the financial norms or 50 % of
the expenditure incurred by thereon for supplementary nutrition whichever is less. Financial norms for supplementary nutrition
fixed in 1991 have been revised in October, 2004, for children from 6 months to 6 years, Rs. 2.00 per day per child and for
severely malnourished children, Rs. 2.70 per child per day.  On  a specific query about the number of children covered under
ICDS and getting nutrition, the Committee was informed that as per Census 2001, total number of children in the age group 0-
6 years is 15.78 crores. Of these, 10.49 crore children have been reported as child population as per Anganwadi Survey
Register under ICDS as on 30.09.06.  The Committee is, however, surprised to note that only 5.43 crore children out of 10.49
crore children under ICDS were getting supplementary nutrition as on 30.09.06.  Such a huge gap between targeted children
and those covered under ICDS and between children under ICDS and getting supplementary nutrition depicts a very dismal
scenario.  If the State-wise figures are analysed, shortfall and gaps are noticed across the country. The Committee is extremely 
disturbed to note that there are States where need is the maximum, but out of less than half of targeted children covered under
ICDS, only 50 per cent are getting the benefit of supplementary nutrition.
 
Action Taken
 
As on 31.3.2007, 10.76 crore children have been reported as child population as per Anganwadi Survey Registers
under ICDS.  Of these, 5.82 crore children were getting supplementary nutrition.  The Ministry is reviewing regularly and
monitoring the progress of coverage of beneficiaries.  State-wise details are given in Annexure-V.  State Governments have
been requested to register all the children (0-6 years) at the AWCs and provide the services under the Scheme.  22 States have
provided supplementary nutrition to more than 50% of targeted children, whereas remaining 13 States have provided less than
50% of child population covered under AWCs.

Recommendations/Observations
 
Para 11.2         Committee’s experience about new schemes proposed to be launched by the Ministry has not been very
encouraging. Committee has been observing that new schemes are proposed without any preliminary exercise about
formulation of their components.  A token provision is duly made which continues for years together due to a number of
procedural formalities to be completed at different levels. New schemes should be announced only after the text of the scheme
is ready.  Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and Children and Scheme for Relief and
Rehabilitation of Rape Victims are two such schemes. Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and
Children was introduced during the Tenth Plan.  As per the information available with the Committee, there was an allocation
of Rs. 3.00 crore for the Scheme in 2004-05, reduced to Rs. 30 lakhs in 2005-06 and Rs. 50 lakhs provided in 2006-07.
Provision for 2007-08 is Rs. 1.00 crore. The only progress which seems to have been made is the change in its name. The very
fact that it is proposed to be launched as a new scheme inspite of being in the formulation stage during the Tenth Plan indicates
that there is not going to be any progress in the near future.  Scheme for Relief and Rehabilitation  of Rape Victims is the other
scheme which was introduced in 2006-07 with a token provision of Rs. 1.00 crore. Same provision is there for 2007-08 and it
continues to be at the proposal stage.
 
Action Taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted. So far as Comprehensive Scheme for Combating
Trafficking of Women & Children is concerned,  the EFC meeting has already taken place and minutes circulated to all
concerned. The final approval of Ministry of Finance is awaited before the scheme is formally launched. As regard the scheme
on ‘Relief and Rehabilitation of Rape Victims”, in principal approval from for the scheme from the Planning Commission is
still awaited. Hence, provisions made could not be utilized.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            The Committee has been voicing its deep concern on the practice of launching/announcing of new schemes and their
remaining in formulation stage.  The Committee finds that approach of the Ministry remains unchanged.  The Committee had
highlighted the status of two new schemes in its earlier report.  The Committee is constrained to observe that those two
schemes, ie Comprehensive Scheme for Combating Trafficking of Women and Children and Scheme for Relief and

Para 11.4         The Committee has noted that the problem of malnutrition being multi-sectoral is being tackled by as many as
10 schemes/ programmes under different Ministries of the Government of India.  The Committee was informed that a National
Level Coordination Committee consisting of representatives from all concerned Ministries has been constituted in the year
2005 under the chairmanship of Minister of WCD to coordinate the various schemes.  The Committee may be apprised about
the number of meetings held by the Coordination Committee since its inception and the initiatives taken by them to have a
coordinated approach to tackle the problem of malnutrition.
 
Action Taken
 
The Coordination and Advisory Committee on ICDS Scheme at the National level was set up during the year 2005
under the Chairpersonship of Secretary (WCD).  Though, only one meeting of the Coordination Committee at National level
has been held, consistent efforts have been made by the Government to ensure effective convergence of delivery of services. 
Some of the steps taken in this direction include:
 
issue of a joint letter under the signature of Secretary (WCD) and Secretary (H&FW) to all the States/UTs, defining the
role and responsibilities of Auxillary Nurse Midwife (ANM) and Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA), who are
the key health functionaries at the grass roots level and Anganwadi Workers (AWW), the core ICDS functionary.
Instructions to States for setting up of Coordination Committees at State, District, Block and village level to ensure
effective delivery of services under ICDS in conjunction with the line Ministries/Departments viz.  Ministry of Rural
Development for total sanitation Campaign and Swajaldhara.  States are also constantly being impressed upon to hold
meetings of these committees at regular intervals.  
 
Setting up of a National Level Monitoring Committee under the Chairpersonship of MOS(WCD) in February, 2007. 
First meeting of this Committee is likely to be held shortly.   
 
Setting up of a Central Monitoring Unit at National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
            Malnutrition continues to afflict both children and young mothers in our country, inspite of this problem being tackled
through schemes administered by a number of Ministries including the Ministry of Women and Child Development.  The
Committee had noted earlier that a National Level Coordination Committee consisting of representatives from all the

I.          INTRODUCTION
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
1.4       In so far as the subject of Sports is concerned, this figures in the State List of the Constitution. In view of this, it is
the State Governments who are primarily responsible for the development and promotion of sports. The Ministry of Youth
Affairs & Sports in its effort to complement the State’s efforts aims at development of a broad based sports culture
throughout the country, and significantly expanding the pool of talented sportspersons who can be groomed to bring
laurels to the country in international events. With this in view, a major initiative proposed to be launched by the Ministry
is a scheme with the title ‘Panchayat Yuva Khel Abhiyan’, which is aimed at creating basic sports infrastructure, and
promoting sports activities at the village/sub-district level, both as a necessary ingredient of youth development and as a
means to substantially widen the catchment for spotting of talent.  The Committee desires that Panchayat Yuva Khel
Abhiyan should be finalized at the earliest and the details in this regard may be furnished to the Committee.  
 
Action Taken
 
            The scheme of Panchayat Yuva Krida Aur Khel Abhiyan (PYKKA) has been approved in principle by Planning
Commission.
 
            Necessary action for the preparation of EFC proposal has been initiated.  A copy of the PYKKA proposal is placed
at Annex-I.
 
 
II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.12     The problem of pending UCs with NGOs, the Committee notes has seen no visible improvement; it, in fact,
appears to be increasing in some schemes. The NGOs that have outstanding UCs need to be blacklisted and the good ones
must be encouraged to come forward in a big way.
 
Action Taken
 
             With a view to streamlining the procedure and bringing in uniformity across the 4 NGO related grants-in-aid
schemes, it was decided to implement the revised procedure w.e.f. 2006-07.  Instructions in this regard were issued to all
the State Governments/UT Administrations dated 1 May 2006. According to this revised procedure, the Ministry is to
invite applications from NGOs after giving advertisement in the newspapers.  The recommending authorities in the
districts are to forward NGOs applications in duplicate to the Secretary (Youth Affairs) in their respective State
Government/UT Administrations after verifications of their antecedents and countersigning the application.  The State
Government/UT Administrations are to constitute a State/UT Level Screening Committee (SLSC) under the Chairmanship
of the Secretary (Youth Affairs) in the State/UT for screening, scrutiny, pre-appraisal, technical feasibility etc. of these
proposals.  The SLSC are to examine the proposals on the basis of technical capability, availability of infrastructure,
trained manpower for the proposed activity and past performance/credibility of the NGO including their financial
soundness, non-involvement in the anti-social or anti-national activities.  The SLSC are to shortlist a limited number of
proposals and prioritize before they are forwarded by the State Government in a single copy to the Government of India
scheme wise.
 
            This revised procedure adopted in 2005-06 has resulted in getting better quality proposals and also much lesser in
number (in hundreds in place of in thousands). The priority accorded by the State/UT was strictly followed so as to avoid
any discretion. Since States/UTs were involved in the forwarding they were also requested to monitor and provide
assistance wherever needed in making the programmes success. As a result between 60-70% of the grantees sanctioned in
2005-06 came back for 2
nd installment within the year itself. The ministry has taken a proactive step of reminding the
remaining NGOs who have not submitted UCs so far.
 
With effect from current financial year i.e. 2007-08 the following measures have been taken to further streamline the

process:-
-           NGOs have also been asked to give their bank account number so that the grant can be transferred in their accounts
through ECS.  This has been done so that no bogus or fake NGO can receive grant.  It would also speed up the

The framework for implementation of SSA is not an area specific document but is applicable throughout India. However,

VII.     OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.1       The Committee notes that the problems of North Eastern States are peculiar which are different from those in rest
of the country. Apart from low level of economic development, these States including J&K are faced with large scale law
and order problems including militancy. Most of the States are not in a position to release their share due to their limited
revenue base. The pace of construction of school buildings and additional class-rooms, toilets etc. is quite slow. The per
unit construction cost is very high due to the difficult terrains, harsh climate and inaccessibility of human habitations.
Transportation of goods & materials to schools makes every thing highly expensive. In fact even within the sanctioned
project area, the programme does not reach every settlement. Many of these States are using funds under PMGY
(Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana) to substitute rather than supplement the funds allocated.
 
Action Taken
 
It is fact that the pace of construction of civil works activities in comparatively slower due to transportation bottleneck,
harsh climate, law and order problems including insurgency. The per unit construction cost is governed under influence of
above stated factors.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.2       Most of the States have, therefore, demanded that the funding pattern for NE States may be revised to 90:10
between the Centre and the States. The Committee feels that their demands needs serious consideration, particularly in
view of the small internal revenue base of the North Eastern States & J&K. The Committee also recommends that the per
unit cost of civil works may be revised keeping in view the difficult terrain/geographical conditions of these States. The
Committee wishes to point out that the problem of increasing amount of State-share every year is due to increase in annual

allocation for SSA every year. Some NE States, therefore, demanded that it should be made hundred per cent centrally
funded scheme. In view of this, the Committee also feels that feasibility of this proposal deserves serious consideration.
 
Action Taken
 
The Central Government has now prescribed a funding pattern of 90:10 for implementation of SSA programme in North
Eastern States during XIth Plan.
The Govt. of India is not determining the unit cost of construction of school building, additional classroom, drinking water
and toilets etc. The unit cost of these items is based on Basic Schedule Rates (BSR) of State Public Works Deptt. The State
Govt. is allowed to determine unit cost on the basis of BSR. Therefore, it is unlikely that construction cost of SSA is high
in comparison to works carry out by Works Deptt. of State”.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
7.4       The Committee notes with concern that, of the total out-of-school children in the country, 10 per cent are from the
NE States. Another aspect of concern in the North Eastern States is the high drop-out rate; it is as high as 71 per cent in
some States. The Gross Enrolment Ratio, however, is fairly good in this region. Similarly, the pupil teacher ratio in the
North East is also better than the national average. Against a national desirable ratio of 1:40, Arunachal Pradesh has a
ratio of 1:27, Assam has 1:22, Mizoram 1:19, Nagaland 1:12, Sikkim 1:12 and Tripura has 1:23. Yet another area of
concern is the appointment of teachers. The North Eastern States have so far appointed only 5204 teachers, which is
roughly about 34 per cent of the total sanctioned; 66% are yet to be appointed. Besides, the North Eastern States have a
very large number of untrained teachers. The Committee was further informed that the assistance of IGNOU is being
taken for training the teachers through distance education mode.

from provincial, Govt. Recognized LP & UP schools for the period from 1999 to 2006. As per the findings of this cohort

III.       IMPLEMENTATION OF ICDS IN J&K
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
3.4       The Committee notes that spread of Anganwadi centers in J&K was uneven as well as inadequate; all the
settlements/habitations were yet to be covered under ICDS. Mechanism of monitoring is very poor; large number of fake
Anganwadis were reported that existed only on paper.  The Committee is aware that parts of State, particularly the valley
is facing twin problems of militancy and under-development.  The problems are complex but not insurmountable. 
Ultimately the women and children are suffering and the benefits of this scheme were not reaching them.  The Committee,

205th COMMITTEE ON HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT

therefore, has come to the conclusion that a more concerted effort, well thought-out and better- planned strategy needs to
be chalked out to tackle the problems afflicting the implementation of the ICDS scheme in the State.  The Anganwadi
workers are the agents of social change; they should be equipped and motivated to achieve the proclaimed objectives of
ICDS. To achieve this, the Committee recommends to ensure that the honorarium was paid to them in time and their
problems/grievances must be considered in sympathetic manner.  There is a strong case to consider giving higher amount
of honorarium and better working conditions to them who are daring the terrorists and harsh climate in the difficult and
inaccessible areas of J&K. 
 
Action Taken
 
Government of India is fully conscious of the significance of the voluntary efforts put in by the Anganwadi workers and
Helpers.  Continuous efforts have been made to improve their working conditions by extending facilities such as paid
absence on maternity, insurance cover under the Anganwadi Karyakartri Bima Yojana, reservation of 25% of vacant posts
of Supervisors for Anganwadi Workers, recruitment of 25% of Anganwadi Workers from Anganwadi Helpers etc.
As per the ICDS guidelines, all States and UTs are required to set up Grievance Redressal Committees to enable redressal
of grievances of AWWs/AWHs.   As per the information available, Grievance Redressal Committees have been formed in
19 States/UTs, till February, 2006.
Government of India has also issued instructions to States/UTs to ensure that the honorarium to AWWs/AWHs is paid in
time.        
Further, the Government of India constituted a Review Committee to examine the current levels of honorarium and related
issues of Anganwadi Workers & Helpers.  The Committee has submitted its report to the Government and the same is
under examination. 
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee finds that the Ministry has not responded to the alleged running of fake AWCs only on paper causing huge
loss to the exchequer. It is perhaps due to absence of an efficacious monitoring system. The Committee urges the Ministry
to evolve strategies taking into consideration the local needs and considerations of the State.  The Committee, therefore,
reiterates that vigorous and concerted efforts need to be made for successful functioning of the AWCs in J&K.
The Committee notes that 19 States/UTs have set up Grievance Redressal Committees to enable redressal of grievances of
AWWs/AWHs.  The Committee would also like to know the reasons for non-setting up of Grievance Redressal
Committees in the remaining States/UTs. It recommends the Ministry to pursue the matter with these States/UTs.  Further,
adequate publicity must be given about Grievance Redressal Committee so that aggrieved persons can approach the
Committee for the redressal of their grievances.
 
Recommendation/Observations
 
3.5       In J&K, large number of Anganwadi Centres do not have permanent buildings.  The Committee notes that the
recent earthquake has also damaged many of the Anganwadi Centers.  After the earthquake, Government of India has
offered a large package for reconstruction of the earthquake affected areas.  The Committee, recommends that the Ministry
of WCD should obtain fund from the disaster management scheme not only for the reconstruction of all the damaged
Anganwadis in J&K but also for constructing permanent Anganwadi buildings for those Anganwadis which are
functioning from temporary buildings.
 
Action Taken
 
As far as construction of Anganwadi buildings is concerned there is no such provision at present for release of funds for
this purpose to the States except to the North Eastern States out of NER component of the budget of the Ministry.  Some
construction has also been undertaken in states covered under the World Bank assisted ICDS Projects.  However, a

The ICDS Scheme does not provide for construction of Anganwadi buildings except in World Bank Assisted Projects. 
However, keeping in view the special needs of North Eastern States, the Central Government sanctioned construction of
AWCs from the year 2001. From 2005, this activity was integrated with the main ICDS Scheme and the Government of
India decided to support NE States in construction of AWCs to the extent of availability of funds out of the 10% funds
earmarked for NE region in the budget of the Ministry. 
 
Though J&K was not covered under World Bank Assisted ICDS I/II/APER Projects, construction was entrusted to the

date

Kashmir also as in the case of the North-Eastern States. The Committee expects the State to settle the accounts in respect

10.5.2  The pay structure of ICDS functionaries, the Committee came to know, differed from State to State in the region.
During the successive pay revisions from 1995, till date, the pay structure of the ICDS functionaries of Manipur had

the delayed release of fund, the salaries and honorarium of ICDS functionaries remained unpaid. This not only causes
hardships to ICDS functionaries but also affects performance of the scheme. To avoid this, it was suggested that the State
Governments may make regular payment of salaries and honorarium to the ICDS functionaries that may be adjusted later
from the funds released by the Union Government.

All ICDS functionaries, except AWWs & AWHs who are honorary workers, are borne on the State Cadre. Their salaries

pattern under Special Nutrition Programme be revised to 90:10 between the Centre and the States instead of 50:50 at 
present.

own resources.  As some of the States were finding it difficult to meet this obligation, it has been decided to provide grant-
in-aid to States/UTs to the extent of 50% of the financial norms for supplementary nutrition or 50% of the actual

I.       BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
1.1     The Department projected a requirement of Rs.40762 crores for the various schemes concerning
School Education and Literacy.  Against this projection, a plan allocation of Rs. 26,800 crores has been
provided in BE 2008-09.  The Committee was informed that this year's allocation is Rs.4,609 crores
(20.77%) more than the RE allocation of Rs.22,191 crores in 2007-08.

2007-08 and 2008-09 as follows:-

1.3     The Committee observes that while there is a marginal decrease in the allocation for Sarva Shiksha
Abhiyan in 2008-09 as compared to 2007-08 allocations, all the other sectors/schemes show an upward
trend with the major share of it going to the Secondary Education followed by Mid-Day Meal Scheme,
Adult Education and Secondary education. The Committee would, however, like to point out that out
of Rs. 13,100 crore allocated for SSA in 2008-09, Rs. 7690.00 crores is proposed to be met from the
amount generated as Education Cess under the Prarambhik Shiksha Kosh against the
contribution of Rs. 6993.00 crore as Education Cess in 2007-08.  Similarly, under MDM Scheme,
out of Rs. 8000.00 crore allocated for 2008-09, Rs. 5127.00 crore is envisaged from the Education
Cess, as compared to contribution of Rs. 3400.00 crore from Education Cess in 2007-08.  Thus, it is
evident that direct funding by the Central Government to its two flagship Schemes of Sarva
Shiksha Abhiyan and MDM was, in fact, declining as there was simultaneous increase in the
amount accruing from Educational Cess that goes to Prarambhik Shiksha Kosh.
 
1.4     The Committee was informed that the enhancement in the allocation for the Mid-Day meal
Scheme was on account of its extension to the Upper Primary level all over the country. Under
Secondary education, raise in allocation was mainly for the proposed two new schemes viz., 'New Model
Schools' and 'Upgradation of 2000 Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (Residential schools,
Hostels/Girls Hostels)'.  Under the Adult Education, one new programme named 'Literacy Programme
for 35+ age group' was proposed to be introduced in the current fiscal.   The Committee welcomes the
extension of MDM to upper primary level and launching of new schemes for girls’ and also for 35+
persons. 
 
Under-utilization of Funds
 
1.5     The Committee notes that during the previous fiscal, under the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, till mid-
February 2008, only Rs.10,689.98 crore was spent out of the Rs.13,171 crores.  Similarly, for the Mid-
Day Meal Scheme, reported expenditure during this period was Rs.5670.71 crores against the allocation
of Rs.6678 crores as in March, 2008. In the Adult Education sector also, expenditure was to the tune of
Rs.212.33 crores against an allocation of Rs.251 crores as on 29
th February, 2008. Such under-
utilization in the case of SSA & MDM during 2007-08 notwithstanding, the Committee notes
improvement in the rate of increase in the utilization of allocations as compared to the previous
years.  The Committee recommends that every possible effort should be made for narrowing this
gap in the utilisation of allocated funds to the maximum possible extent.
 
Pending Utilisation Certicates (UCs)
 
1.6     Problem of large number of pending Utilisation Certificates is another issue engaging Committee's
attention. The Committee also notes the problem of unspent balances available with the implementing
agencies.  As on 31
st December, 2007, a total of 1265 Utilisation Certificates amounting to Rs. 995.40
crores were not received in respect of Grants/loan released upto the 31 st March, 2006.  Further, total
unspent balances with implementing agencies under different schemes as on the 1 st April, 2007 was Rs.
3637.71 crores, which increased to the tune of Rs. 5465.58 crores in the next six months i.e., on the 30th
September, 2007.  The Committee notes that Unspent Balances were available with implementing

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/206th%20Report%20of%20School%20Education%20&%20Literacy.htm[01-07-2016 15:48:53]
agencies (other than State Government/UTs) mainly in the Voluntary Sector.  The Committee was
informed that efforts were being made to get the UCs expedited and some progress had been made and a
large number of NGOs had been blacklisted.  The Committee feels concerned about a large amount
of funds being cornered by these bodies and no efforts being made to get the money back from
them.  The only action taken against the erring NGOs is to blacklist them.  The Committee
recommends that every effort be made to bring them to book and such NGOs be proceeded
against under the Indian Penal Code.
 
II.      SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN
 
2.1     Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is the national flagship programme launched in 2001-02 for
achieving the goal of Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE) through a time bound approach in
partnership with States and Local Bodies.  It is also an attempt to provide an opportunity for improving
capabilities of all the children in the age group of 6-14 years through provision of community-based
quality education in a mission mode. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan today covers all States and Union
territories, reaching out to 19.4 crore children in 12.3 lakh habitations.
Achievements under SSA
 
2.2     The achievements of SSA have been stated to be as follows :-
 
Activity Achievement

2.3     The Committee is fully aware of the various limitations in the gigantic task of
universalisation of elementary education (UEE) in a vast country like ours particularly, through
the schemes like SSA and MDM. It appreciates the efforts made in trying to achieve various goals

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/206th%20Report%20of%20School%20Education%20&%20Literacy.htm[01-07-2016 15:48:53]
set in this regard and the Committee takes note of some improvements in respect of various
dimensions/indicators towards reaching the goal of UEE.  It, however, feels its duty to point out
the areas of concern with a view to making mid way corrections and making assiduous efforts for
achieving our goal in time.
 
Goals of SSA
 
2.4     The Committee would like to draw attention towards the main targets of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan
which are as follow:-
Ø
     All children in school, Education Guarantee Centre, Alternate School, ‘Back-to-School’ camp by
2005
Ø     Bridge all gender and social category gaps at primary stage by 2007 and at upper primary level by
2010
Ø      Universal retention by 2010
Ø     Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis an education for life.
 
2.5     The Committee notes that the first goal of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan to bring all children to
schools, Education Guarantee Centres, Alternate Schools, ‘Back-to-School’ camps by 2005 has
been long overdue. As per District Information System for Education (DISE) 2006-07 figures, the
Net Enrolment Ratio (NER) at the primary level and the Upper Primary level stands at 92.75 and
48.45 respectively. Further, as per the Department's estimate, around 75.97 lakh children in the
age group of 6-14 do not attend any form of schooling.  Maximum concentration of such children
is reported to be in Bihar (28%) followed by West Bengal (18%) and Uttar Pradesh (10%).   Even
after three years since 2005, the goal of achieving universal enrolment remains yet to be achieved.
 
2.6     As regards bridging gender and social gaps at primary level by 2007 and upper primary
level by 2010, the situation is no better. As per the target, we should have by now been able to
bridge the gender and social gaps at primary level. However, DISE 2006-07 statistics puts the
Gender Parity Index in enrolment at 0.93 for the primary level. On the social front, percentage of
enrolment at elementary level is 19.87 for SCs and 10.69 for STs. For OBCs, it is 42.18 % at the
primary level and 41.23 % at the upper primary level. Going at this pace, it is highly unlikely that
the goal of bridging gender and social gaps in elementary education can be achieved by the year
2010.
 
2.7     The goal of Universal Retention by 2010 also, it appears, would remain unfulfilled.  The
drop-outs rate of primary level in the Class I-V group has, no doubt, decreased from 39% in 2001
to 29% in 2004-05; it still might be about 20%.  State-wise figures, however, indicate extreme
disparities in this respect.  There are ten States having a dropout rate exceeding 40%. In contrast
Delhi, Puducherry and Kerala show 0% dropout rate, followed by six States having less than 5%
dropout rate.  This rate was more than 60% at upper primary and secondary levels in 2004-05.
Going at this rate, the target of universal retention by 2010 appears difficult to reach.
 
2.8     For girls, the dropout rate has remained around 25.4% in 2005. Similarly, SC and ST
student dropout rates have been 34.2% and 42.3% respectively.   And if drop-out rate is taken as
total for class I to VIII, it was around 50% in the year 2004-05.  Comparative analysis of State-

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/206th%20Report%20of%20School%20Education%20&%20Literacy.htm[01-07-2016 15:48:53]
wise achievement level points out to another disturbing trend.  In respect of quite a few States,
dropout rate shows an upward trend during the period 2002-05.  Not only this, in respect of some
States, whereas enrolment ratio continues to be much below the national ratio, drop-out rate is
considerably higher than the average rate.  Thus, the Committee feels that the target of the
Universal Retention by the year 2010 also would be difficult to reach.
 
2.9     The following figures were made available to the Committee in respect of the SSA:

2.10   The Committee notes that under all these components, some of the works are under construction
also.  Even then, considerable gap is there between the targets set and achievements made, with
disparities being noticed in State-wise figures.  Besides this, the Committee is surprised to note that
exact details and status of all the targets are not there.  In majority of the cases, construction works
completed and in progress do not match with the cumulative targets. The Committee would appreciate
if exact status note is made available to it.   
 
2.11   Likewise, there is a big gap between teachers to be recruited and trained. Against overall target of
11,34,068, teachers recruited upto 31.12.2007 were 8,62,399, with maximum shortfall noticed in respect
of Bihar, Chattishgarh, Jammu & Kashmir, Jharkhand, Karnataka,  Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and West
Bengal.  
 
2.12   The Committee is of the view that the slow pace of progress in providing basic infrastructure
in the schools is a major problem area.  The main goals of SSA can only be achievable if basic
components like school building, additional classrooms, drinking water, toilet facilities,
recruitment and training of teachers were in place as scheduled. These gaps under different
components of SSA were being persistently pointed out by the Committee.  With the availability of
funds and effective monitoring mechanism reported to be in place, position should have improved
by now.  The Committee would again emphasize that the basic infrastructure as well as dedicated
teachers are the deciding factors through which SSA goals and targets can be accomplished in
time.
 
Quality in SSA
 
2.13   Last but not the least, the quality of elementary education being provided in the government
and government-aided schools, let alone EGS/AIE centres, leaves much to be desired.  In the
absence of clearly identified verifiable indicators of quality, the quality of education could be
judged mainly on the basis of the students learning achievement levels. As per the findings of the
2003-04 National Sample Survey by NCERT for class III which was carried out in 29 States,
students in as many as 17 States scored below the mean achievement level in Mathematics and 13

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/206th%20Report%20of%20School%20Education%20&%20Literacy.htm[01-07-2016 15:48:53]
States were lagging being in achievement in Language. For Class V covering 30 States/UTs,
students of 17 and 15 States/UTs scored below the mean achievement levels in mathematics and
languages respectively. Class VIII students of as many as 10 States (in mathematics), 11 States (in
languages) and 10 States (in Science) scored below the mean achievement levels in a survey
conducted across 17 States. Further, as per DISE 2006-07 figures, only 44.96% boys and 45.12 %
girls could pass the class IV/V examinations with 60% and above marks. The figures for classes
VII/VIII are 38.83% for boys and 40.06% for girls. Clearly, the achievement levels of students are
far from being satisfactory. 
 
2.14   The Committee is of the view that one of the reasons for the lack of quality education in the
elementary schools is the teachers themselves not possessing the required academic qualifications. 
Committee's apprehensions are borne out by the DISE data of 2006-07, which showed that only
44.01% regular elementary school teachers possess qualification upto Higher Secondary level with
some of the States having teachers with still lower qualifications.  The Committee can only imagine
about the status of teachers in EGS/AIE Centres.   
 
2.15   The Committee expresses its grave concern on the aforesaid findings. At the current pace of
progress being made towards the goal of universalisation of elementary education, the Committee
has serious doubts about achieving the goals by the year 2010. The Committee, therefore,
recommends to the Department to make a realistic assessment of the progress made vis-a-vis the
targets on priority basis. Based on the findings of the assessment, the Department could consider
redefining the goals/targets of the scheme in a realistic manner.
         
Funding Pattern
 
2.16   Sharing of funds under the programme of SSA was on an 85:15 basis during the Ninth Plan and
75:25 during the Tenth Plan between the Centre and the States. The envisaged 50:50 sharing
arrangement after the Tenth Plan is proposed to be achieved in a phased manner during the Eleventh
Plan. The Department proposes to bring down the Central share in phases, to 65:35 during the first two
years (i.e, 2007-08 and 2008-09); 60:40 in the third year (i.e, 2009-10) ; 55:45 in the fourth year (i.e,
2010-11); and 50:50 thereafter i.e, from 2011-12 onwards.

further in coming years, it may be difficult for the States and UTs to spare 50% of the total SSA
allocations. The Committee has been informed that all the States and UTs were now contributing their
share regularly.   It indicates their increasing commitment to SSA and its goals.  The Committee is
happy to note this.  On a note of caution, it however, would like to emphasize that inability of any
State/UT to contribute the required share might hamper the achievements made under SSA. The
Committee, therefore, feels that the sharing pattern suggested by the Working Group is worth
considering.

Educational Guarantee Scheme (EGS) and Alternative & Innovative Education (AIE) under SSA
 
2.23   Under the Education Guarantee Scheme (EGS), educational facilities are set up in habitations that
do not have a primary school within a distance of one km. Any habitation having 25 out of school

children in the 6-14 age group (15 in the case of hilly and desert areas and tribal hamlets) is eligible to
have an EGS centre. The EGS is a transitory facility till a primary school replaces it in two years. Formal
curriculum is taught in EGS centres and all enrolled children are provided free textbooks and mid day
meal. The EGS is managed by the local community bodies viz. Parent Teacher Association (PTA),
Village Education Committee (VEC) or the Gram Panchayats. A local teacher is engaged by the
community for teaching in such centres.
 
2.24   Under the AIE component, flexible strategies are being implemented for education of children
who cannot be directly enrolled in a school/EGS centre. The strategies include residential and non-
residential bridge courses, back to school camps, seasonal hostels, drop-in centres and other alternative
schools. AIE has been more effective in providing education to the older age group (11-14 years) never
enrolled or dropout children, children who migrate seasonally with their families, street and other
deprived urban children, working children and other vulnerable children in difficult circumstances.
 
2.25   Till December 2007, 95493 EGS centres had been upgraded to primary schools. In 2007-08, 7.1
lakh children were enrolled in 18268 EGS centres till December, 2007. Another 29.26 lakh children had
been enrolled in 58392 AIE centres till December, 2007. 3497 residential bridge course centres and 7367
centres for urban deprived children and for children belonging to migrating families had been provided
upto December, 2007.  The Committee, however, notes that targets set for AIE coverage for 2006-07
remained unfulfilled.  Against targetted 59,19,685 children to be covered under AIE Centres, only
30,32,943 children could be covered.  Position remained unchanged during 2007-08 also.  Against
the target of 47,44,701 children to be brought under AIE centres, after first three quarters, achievement
was only 29,26,619 children.   The Committee understands that these children are from the 'very
hard to reach' category.  But the fact remains that in many States, there are large number of such
children deprived of any education so far.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the
Department should make every endeavour to actively involve the concerned State Government to
bridge such glaring gaps.
 
2.26   The Committee is aware of the need of EGS and AIE in our context and appreciates the
upgradation of these to Primary Schools.  Around 24 lakh children are still in this system.  Our
effort must be to phase out these centres at the earliest because after all these are not full-fledged
schools. While EGS/AIE may be helpful in achieving universal access, their quality of education
would not be at par with the formal schools.
 
Girl's Education under SSA
 
2.27   SSA promotes girls education to equalise educational opportunities and eliminate gender
disparities. SSA has made efforts to mainstream gender concerns in all the activities under the
programme. A two pronged strategy adopted for the promotion of girls education is to make the
education system responsive to the needs of girls on the one hand and to generate a community demand
for girls education, on the other. A focused strategy has now been made in education planning to target
low female literacy pockets and reduce gender disparity. Special effort is being made to bring the out-of-
school girls, especially from the disadvantaged sections to the schools. Girls education is targetted
through National Programme for Girls Education at Elementary Level and Kasturba Gandhi Balika
Vidyalaya (KGBV).
